Mechanisms of MPNST Metastasis
# Mechanisms of MPNST Metastasis
## CTF - Young Investigator Award
### Principal Investigator: Alexa Sheehan
### Project Lead / Data Coordinator: Alexa Sheehan
### Institution: University of Iowa
### Project Description:
Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs) are aggressive, highly metastatic sarcomas with poor clinical prognoses. Treatment of this cancer, especially when it metastasizes, has not improved over the last 30 years. Therefore, there is a critical need to further understand and target key aspects of MPNST progression to develop effective treatment options. The overall goal of this study is to identify and disrupt mechanisms of MPNST metastasis using novel therapeutics to ultimately improve outcomes for patients. We will utilize recently developed pharmaceutical agents to determine if inhibiting the function of lysyl oxidase enzymes can decrease MPNST metastasis. Lysyl oxidases (Lox) are proteins that modify the extracellular environment of tumor cells. Recently, we demonstrated that the expression of Loxs increases in MPNST cells that have loss-of-function mutations in the genetic regulator PRC2. Loss of PRC2 is also associated with increased metastasis in both mouse models and patients and we have determined that inhibiting Lox activity can significantly restrict this process (PMID 36066973). In this study, we will assess the ability of newer formulations of Lox inhibitors to decrease MPNST metastasis in our preclinical models. These next-generation agents are more specific and less toxic than previous versions and are currently being tested in clinical trials for fibrotic disease and some cancer types. We predict that these therapeutics will inhibit MPNST metastasis and could represent a promising treatment option for patients. Additionally, PRC2 loss is associated with global reprogramming of gene expression in MPNST. These changes result in increased expression of proteins that promote tumor growth, however they also induce instability which makes cells more sensitive to certain drugs that further enhance this state. These drugs, known as epigenetic modulators, inhibit growth of MPNST cells in vitro but have not been tested for their effects on metastasis. In this study, we will treat PRC2-deleted cells with a variety of these agents to determine their impact on cellular invasion and metastatic capabilities. We hypothesize that these modulators will restrict metastasis by decreasing expression of Lox enzymes. If this relationship is observed, will with combine epigenetic therapy with next-generation Lox inhibitors to assess if this further inhibits MPNST metastasis. Overall, we will use a variety of preclinical models to determine if increased Lox expression induced by PRC2 loss is a targetable treatment option for patients with metastatic MPNST.

hits.description:
**Tumorigenesis and Metastasis Analysis**

**Overview**

[Tumorigenesis and Metastasis Analysis](https://www.alfacytology.com/3d-cancer-models/tumorigenesis-and-metastasis-analysis.html) is a fundamental area of cancer research dedicated to understanding the biological mechanisms that drive tumor initiation, progression, invasion, and metastatic dissemination. Tumorigenesis involves the transformation of normal cells into malignant cells through the accumulation of genetic, epigenetic, and microenvironmental alterations, while metastasis represents the spread of cancer cells from the primary tumor to distant organs. Together, these processes are responsible for the majority of cancer-related mortality and remain central topics in oncology research.

This resource provides an overview of research approaches for investigating tumorigenesis and metastasis using advanced three-dimensional tumor models and integrated biological analyses. By combining physiologically relevant experimental systems with molecular, cellular, and functional characterization, researchers can better understand the mechanisms governing tumor development, metastatic progression, and therapeutic response, supporting both basic cancer research and translational oncology studies.

**Research Focus**

Tumorigenesis and Metastasis Analysis encompasses the investigation of multiple biological processes associated with cancer progression, including uncontrolled cell proliferation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), tumor cell migration, invasion, metastatic colonization, and interactions within the tumor microenvironment. Research also explores how genetic alterations, signaling pathways, extracellular matrix remodeling, immune regulation, angiogenesis, and stromal components collectively contribute to tumor progression and metastatic potential.

Studies may further examine the roles of cancer stem cells, tumor heterogeneity, cell-cell communication, and molecular biomarkers associated with metastatic disease. Integrating three-dimensional tumor models with imaging technologies, molecular profiling, and functional assays enables researchers to characterize the dynamic events involved in tumor initiation and metastasis while identifying potential therapeutic targets and predictive biomarkers for cancer treatment.

**Applications**

Tumorigenesis and Metastasis Analysis supports a broad range of oncology research applications, including cancer biology, metastasis research, tumor microenvironment characterization, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) studies, biomarker discovery, drug target validation, mechanism-of-action studies, precision oncology, and preclinical drug development. These research approaches also facilitate investigations into metastatic mechanisms, tumor invasion, therapeutic resistance, and the evaluation of novel anticancer therapies.

As research into tumor initiation and metastatic progression continues to evolve, physiologically relevant experimental models have become increasingly valuable for reproducing complex tumor biology and disease progression. Comprehensive tumorigenesis and metastasis analysis provides researchers with more predictive experimental systems for translational cancer research and contributes to the discovery of innovative therapeutic strategies aimed at preventing cancer progression and metastatic spread.

${image?fileName=combinedLogo%5FwithTitle%2Epng&align=Center&responsive=true}

Metastasis remains the principal cause of mortality among cancer patients. For a tumor cell to metastasize, it must escape the primary tumor, successfully negotiate various molecular and cellular interactions, and colonize a new microenvironment to establish a secondary tumor. To predict how and when cancer will metastasize and to develop more effective treatments, a better understanding is needed about how these individual events - tumor growth, dissemination, colonization, and survival - contribute to the complex metastatic process. Recent advances in live-cell imaging, characterization of circulating tumor cells, experimental models of tumor dormancy, descriptions of tumor cell – immune system crosstalk, cell and tissue mechanics, and single-cell genomic and proteomic analysis have provided quantitative data that can be used to build testable mathematical and computational models of tumor metastasis. 
 
The Interdisciplinary Approaches to Cancer Metastasis workshop, to be held **June 12-14, 2017**, in Seattle, WA at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center, will bring together ~25 early stage investigators (within 15 years of terminal degree) across four NCI-supported programs, the Innovative Molecular Analysis Technologies ([IMAT](https://imat.cancer.gov)) program, the Informatics Technology for Cancer Research ([ITCR](https://itcr.nci.nih.gov)) program, the Cancer Systems Biology Consortium ([CSBC](http://csbconsortium.org)) and the Physical Sciences-Oncology Network ([PS-ON](https://physics.cancer.gov)), along with select outside investigators to tackle important questions in cancer metastasis. The goal is to form teams that utilize the technologies and computational approaches championed by IMAT and ITCR along with the cancer systems biology and physical oncology viewpoints employed within the CSBC and PS-ON. Teams will nucleate around a question in cancer metastasis that can best be addressed through an interdisciplinary approach.
 
Discussions at the workshop will be guided by distinguished scientist “[Mentors](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/wiki/408136),” who will assist in articulating project ideas and facilitate participant discussions both before and during the workshop. Select proposals developed during the Interdisciplinary Approaches to Cancer Metastasis workshop will be selected for funding through a process involving workshop participants, scientific Mentors, and NCI Program Staff. Specific details about the workshop can be found [here](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/wiki/408139).

About the workshop
The IACM workshop is designed to solicit novel pilot project ideas and distribute funds to one or more **teams** of scientists from diverse institutions and backgrounds.  The workshop itself is divided into three stages, as preparation is required of the attendees before the workshop and follow-up is expected from those attendees who receive the pilot project funds.

###Pre-workshop activities
Ahead of the workshop selected applicants will meet weekly ~6 times to discuss ideas with other attendees and describe ideas via teleconference.  All applicants will gain access to [this Synapse project site](syn7433743) to facilitate discussions and brainstorming in between the meetings and ultimately form teams surrounding select ideas. Selected applicants are expected to:
* Register for a [Synapse account](http://www.synapse.org/register) to gain access
* Attend 6 weekly [virtual meetings](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn9693597) with the other selected attendees and selected mentors
* Initiate discussions in the [discussion forum](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/discussion/default) to identify other candidates to form teams
* Work with those teams begin to discuss project ideas and proposals

###Workshop agenda
Selected applicants are invited to Seattle, WA to participate in the workshop June 12-14, 2017.  This will give the attendees the ability to meet their teammates in person and solidify the project proposal with respect to the pilot project funds. Each team will arrive ready to present their ideas to the group and then refine these ideas and establish a budget throughout the workshop. At the end of the workshop each team will present their proposal to use some or all of the pilot project funds (~\$500,000 in total funds). 
 
All workshop attendees will rank the project proposals and the mentors and meeting organizers will use these rankings to select a final division of funds. Depending on the rankings and proposals, all funds may go to a single collaborative team or be divided among multiple teams. 

A more detailed agenda has been posted on the [IACM attendee page](syn9874222).

###Post-workshop followup
The team(s) selected to receive the pilot project funds will be given 1 year to carry out the research as well as modest travel funds to meet amongst themselves and/or present their ideas. 
Attendee Requirements
This page describes the pre-workshop activities required by invited attendees to the workshop. The goal of these activities is to facilitate the formation of teams that will be ready to kick-off the workshop with a brief presentation of their proposal, which will then be refined over the two-day workshop.
 
Below are the basic steps to get started: 

###Accessing data portal
This [Synapse Project](http://docs.synapse.org/articles/making_a_project.html) will provide ongoing updates for the workshop as we proceed through the planning activities.  You will require access to the full capabilities of this site to participate in [discussions](http://docs.synapse.org/articles/discussion.html) and make use of the [file sharing capabilities](http://docs.synapse.org/articles/versioning.html).  Specifically you will need to:

* Log into synapse using your registered account (make sure you use your first and last name)
* Join the IACM workshop attendee team by clicking the button below:

###Get to know other attendees

###Initiate discussions

###Create team workspace
You can then begin to create folders under the [IACM Project Workspace](syn8063299) folder. Workshop organizers ask that you keep these folders and data available to all workshop attendees while teams are being formed, after which you can create your own synapse projects or private folders to continue planning.

###Teleconference to further discuss ideas
The workshop organizers will host numerous teleconferences that will provide a space for workshop attendees to discuss their ideas with potential team mates as well as workshop organizers.  Links to the teleconferences can be provided [here](syn9693597). 

###Prepare for workshop presentation
The workshop will kick off with presentations from all teams. More details forthcoming.

The workshop is primarily geared toward early stage investigators, designated as those that are within 15 years of a terminal degree*, who are interested in meeting new collaborators and expanding their current research portfolio. Those investigators that do not yet hold an independent position (i.e. postdoctoral fellow or research scientist) are welcome to apply, although if they are not recognized as Principal Investigators by their Institution they likely will not be eligible to receive pilot project funding.Workshop capacity is set at ~25 attendees, who will be selected from the pool of applicants by the NCI representatives, Sage Bionetworks and the [workshop mentors](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/wiki/408136).

## HuR-ELAVL1 drives malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor growth and metastasis.

**Disease Focus:** MPNST (Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumor)
**Assay Types:** Bulk RNA-seq, ChIP-seq
**Species:** Homo sapiens
**Tissue / Cell Type:** MPNST cell lines (ST88-14, ST88)
**Publication:** [PMID:32315290](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32315290/) · [DOI:10.1172/JCI130379](https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI130379)
**Authors:** Marta Palomo-Irigoyen, ..., Ashwin Woodhoo
**Institution:** CIC bioGUNE, Basque Research and Technology Alliance (BRTA)
**Publication Date:** 2020 (JCI)

---

### Summary

This study identifies HuR (ELAVL1), an RNA-binding protein, as a key oncogenic driver in MPNSTs. HuR is highly elevated in human MPNST samples and controls a broad transcriptomic program essential for tumor growth and metastasis. Inhibition of HuR exerts potent cytostatic and cytotoxic effects in MPNST cell lines in vitro and suppresses metastasis in vivo.

---

### Background

Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs) are highly aggressive sarcomas arising from Schwann cell lineage cells. They are strongly metastatic, resistant to chemo- and radiotherapy, and frequently fatal. This work demonstrates that MPNST cells develop a strong addiction to the RNA-binding protein HuR/ELAVL1, which coordinates the expression of multiple oncogenic networks, making it an attractive therapeutic target.

##Tau Immunoprecipitation and Human Postmortem Brain Proteomics

Healthy control (n = 4) and AD patient (n = 4) frontal cortex brain samples (Table S1) were homogenized in NP-40 lysis buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl at pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% NP-40, 5% Glycerol, 5 mM iodoacetamide) with protease and phosphatase inhibitors using a bullet blender according to manufacturer’s instructions followed by centrifugation at 10,000 x g for 15 min at 4°C. Immunoprecipitation was performed as follows, normalizing to 1 mg of total protein from each sample per input: brain lysates were first pre-cleared using Protein A-Sepharose conjugated beads (Invitrogen). Lysates were incubated with 3 mg of anti-Tau monoclonal antibody (TAU-5) overnight at 4°C. Purified Mouse IgG2a K isotype (BD PharMingen) was used as an isotype-matched negative control. 50 mL of Protein G DynaBeads (Invitrogen) beads were incubated with the lysate for 1 hr. Beads were then washed 3 times using wash buffer (50 mM Tris HCl at pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl and 1% NP-40) and rinsed three times using phosphate buffered saline (PBS). A portion of the Dynabeads was subjected to western blot analysis (below) (Figure 1A).
 
The remaining beads were rinsed in PBS (3X) and re-suspended in 500 mL 50 mM NH4HCO3. Proteins bound to beads were reduced using 1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) for 30 min and alkylated with 5 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) for 30 min in darkness. Proteins were digested with 1:100 (w/w) lys-C endopeptidase (Wako) at room temperature for 3 hr followed by further overnight digestion with 1:50 (w/w) trypsin (Promega) at RT. Tryptic peptides were acidified using 1% formic acid and 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid before desalting and purification using C18 StageTip. Peptides were eluted in 50% acetonitrile and were dried using a SpeedVac (Savant). Dried peptides were reconstituted in peptide loading buffer (0.1% formic acid, 0.03% trifluoroacetic acid, 1% acetonitrile). Peptide mixtures were separated by liquid chromatography on a self-packed C18 (1.9 um Dr. Maisch, Germany) fused silica column (25 cm 3 75 mm internal diameter; New Objective, Woburn, MA) by a NanoAcquity UHPLC (Waters, Milford, FA) and monitored on a Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer (ThermoFisher Scientific, San Jose, CA). Elution was performed over a 120-minute gradient at a rate of 400 nL/min with buffer B ranging from 3% to 80% (buffer A: 0.1% formic acid and 5% DMSO in water, buffer B: 0.1% formic and 5% DMSO in acetonitrile). The mass spectrometer cycle was programmed to collect one full MS scan followed by 10 data dependent tandem mass spectrometry MS/MS scans. The MS scans (300–1800 m/z range, 1,000,000 AGC, 150 ms maximum ion time) were collected at a resolution of 70,000 at m/z 200 in profile mode and the MS/MS spectra (2 m/z isolation width, 25% collision energy, 100,000 AGC target, 50 ms maximum ion time) were acquired at a resolution of 17,500 at m/z 200. Dynamic exclusion was set to exclude previous sequenced precursor ions for 30 s within a 10-ppm window. Precursor ions with +1, and +6 or higher charge states were excluded from sequencing.

The MaxQuant (Cox et al., 2014; Luber et al., 2010) (v1.5.5.1) LFQ algorithm was used for protein quantitation as previously described (Seyfried et al., 2017). UniProt protein sequences containing both Swiss-Prot and TrEMBL human protein sequences (90,411 target sequences downloaded April 21, 2015), were duplicated into a reverted (decoy) peptide database, searched, and used to control peptide and razor protein false discovery rate (FDR) at 1% within MaxQuant. Methionine oxidation (+15.9949 Da), asparagine and glutamine deamidation (+0.9840 Da), N-terminal acetylation (+42.0106 Da) and cysteine carbamidomethylation (+57.0215 Da) were assigned as fixed modifications. Tryptic peptides with only 2 mis-cleavages were included in each database search. A precursor mass tolerance of ± 20 ppm was applied prior to mass accuracy calibration and ± 4.5 ppm after internal MaxQuant calibration. Other search settings included a maximum peptide mass of 6,000 Da, a minimum peptide length of 6 residues, 0.05 Da tolerance for high resolution Orbitrap MS/MS scans, or 0.6 Da for low resolution MS/MS scans obtained in the linear ion trap. The FDR for peptide spectral matches, proteins, and site decoy fraction were all set to 1%. Following quantification, missing values were imputed assuming informative missingness such that missing values were replaced with a left Gaussian tail random distribution per parameters previously determined ideal for LFQ based studies (Tyanova et al., 2016). IgG (background) measurements were averaged if either or both AD and control non-specific IgG replicate measurements for summed intensity were non-missing. Otherwise, either non-missing measurement was used; in the case that both measurements were missing (low background), average noise level imputed value for the two IPs was used for background subtraction. Finally, background subtraction (possibly due to differential specificity of the non-specific IgG) was not allowed to produce final values below zero (i.e., negative values were set to zero).

See references as numbered in the [Cell Reports publication](https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/pdf/S2211-1247(19)31166-0.pdf).

# Data Sharing for _Behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia: insights from a multivariate and network-based brain proteome-wide study_

Synapse ID: syn73569657

## Proteomic data
See published manuscript for detailed description of study subjects and proteomic profiling. Briefly, post-mortem dorsolateral prefrontal cortex tissue samples were collected from donors from three cohorts. All donors had a diagnosis of dementia at time of death except for one with a diagnosis of MCI. Samples were processed for proteomic profiling in 23 batches of 17 samples each; batches were randomized for sex, age at death, and post-mortem interval (PMI). Samples were homogenized in 8 M urea lysis buffer, reduced, alkylated, and digested sequentially with Lys‑C and trypsin before being labeled with Tandem Mass Tag (TMT) reagents for multiplexed analysis. After high‑pH offline fractionation into 96 fractions, each fraction was analyzed by FAIMS‑enhanced Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometry using data‑dependent acquisition (120 k MS¹ resolution, 30 k MS² resolution, TurboTMT). Raw TMT files were processed to protein abundances with the FragPipe analysis suite, (version 22.0 with MSFragger version 4.1), which utilizes MSFragger and Philosopher. Raw files were searched against the canonical UniProt human protein database (downloaded February 2019 supplemented with APOE 2 and 4 and Abeta 40 and 42 isoforms: 20,404 total target entries) with the default parameters for TMTPro search: fully tryptic, 2 miscleavages and 20 ppm mass tolerances. The database search yielded data for 11,223 proteins.

## File Descriptions
* Proteomic data - [protein\_compiled\_raw.csv](syn73572886): Protein abundances generated using FragPipe. One row per protein, one column per sample (391 study samples plus 23 global internal standard (GIS) samples).
* Sample IDs - [sample_ids.csv](syn73572633): Maps sample IDs in proteomics data file to IDs that can be used to align data with clinical data. Also includes proteomics batch and post-mortem interval (hours).

###The Consensus Brain Protein Coexpression (ConsensusProteinCoexpression) Study

***Plese cite [Johnson ECB, et al, Nat Med, 2020](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-020-0815-6) when referencing this work and to see additional methods pertaining to the full work.***

#Methods for ALL Brain Tissue Cohorts
###Brain Tissue Samples and Case Classification
Brain tissue used in this study was obtained from the autopsy collections of the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging[1], Banner Sun Health Research Institute[2], Mount Sinai School of Medicine Brain Bank, Adult Changes in Thought Study, Mayo Clinic Brain Bank, Religious Orders Study and Rush Memory and Aging Project[3], University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine Brain Bank, and the Baltimore Coroner’s Office.  Tissue was from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Brodmann Area 9 where available), or temporal cortex and precuneus regions where indicated.  Human postmortem tissues were acquired under proper Institutional Review Board (IRB) protocols at each respective institution.  Postmortem neuropathological evaluation of neuritic plaque distribution was performed according to the Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer’s Disease (CERAD) criteria[4], while extent of spread of neurofibrillary tangle pathology was assessed with the Braak staging system[5].  Other neuropathologic diagnoses were made in accordance with established criteria and guidelines[6, 7].  All case metadata, including age, sex, post-mortem interval, cognitive function, APOE genotype, neuropathological criteria, and disease status, are provided in Supplementary Table 1.  Case classification harmonization across cohorts was performed using the following rubric:  cases with CERAD 0-1 and Braak 0-3 without dementia at last evaluation were defined as control (if Braak equals 3, then CERAD must equal 0); cases with CERAD 1-3 and Braak 3-6 without dementia at last evaluation were defined as AsymAD; cases with CERAD 2-3 and Braak 3-6 with dementia at last evaluation were defined as AD.  Dementia was defined as MMSE <24, CASI score <81, or CDR ≥1, based on prior comparative study[8].  Mayo and UPenn cases were not included in the case harmonization scheme, and therefore preservation of consensus network modules in these cohorts provides an additional degree of robustness.

###Brain Tissue Homogenization and Protein Digestion
Procedures for tissue homogenization for all tissues were performed essentially as described[9, 10].  Approximately 100 mg (wet tissue weight) of brain tissue was homogenize in 8 M urea lysis buffer (8 M urea, 10 mM Tris, 100 mM NaHPO4, pH 8.5) with HALT protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (ThermoFisher) using a Bullet Blender (NextAdvance).  Each Rino sample tube (NextAdvance) was supplemented with ~100 μL of stainless steel beads (0.9 to 2.0 mm blend, NextAdvance) and 500 μL of lysis buffer.  Tissues were added immediately after excision and samples were then placed into the bullet blender at 4 °C.  The samples were homogenized for 2 full 5 min cycles, and the lysates transferred to new Eppendorf Lobind tubes.  Each sample was then sonicated for 3 cycles consisting of 5 s of active sonication at 30% amplitude, followed by 15 s on ice.  Samples were then centrifuged for 5 min at 15,000 x g and the supernatant transferred to a new tube.  Protein concentration was determined by bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay (Pierce).  For protein digestion, 100 μg of each sample was aliquoted and volumes normalized with additional lysis buffer.  For the ROS/MAP cohort, an equal amount of protein from each sample was aliquoted and digested in parallel to serve as the global pooled internal standard (GIS) in each TMT batch, as described below.  Similarly, GIS pooled standards were generated from the Banner, MSSB, Mayo, Aging, and UPenn cohorts.  Samples were reduced with 1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) at room temperature for 30 min, followed by 5 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) alkylation in the dark for another 30 min.  Lysyl endopeptidase (Wako) at 1:100 (w/w) was added and digestion allowed to proceed overnight.  Samples were then 7-fold diluted with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate.  Trypsin (Promega) was then added at 1:50 (w/w) and digestion was carried out for another 16 h.  The peptide solutions were acidified to a final concentration of 1% (vol/vol) formic acid (FA) and 0.1% (vol/vol) trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), and desalted with a 30 mg HLB column (Oasis).  Each HLB column was first rinsed with 1 mL of methanol, washed with 1 mL 50% (vol/vol) acetonitrile (ACN), and equilibrated with 2×1 mL 0.1% (vol/vol) TFA.  The samples were then loaded onto the column and washed with 2×1 mL 0.1% (vol/vol) TFA.  Elution was performed with 2 volumes of 0.5 mL 50% (vol/vol) ACN.

###Mass Spectrometry Analysis for Label-free Proteomics
Mass spectrometry analyses of MSSB, ACT, BLSA, Banner, Mayo, and UPenn cohorts were performed on a Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer essentially as described[10].  Brain-derived tryptic peptides (2 μg) were resuspended in peptide loading buffer (0.1% FA, 0.03% TFA, 1% ACN) containing 0.2 pmol of isotopically labeled peptide calibrants (ThermoFisher 88321).  Peptide mixtures were separated on a self-packed C18 (1.9 μm, Dr. Maisch, Germany) fused silica column (25 cm x 75 μM internal diameter; New Objective, Woburn, MA) by a NanoAcquity UHPLC (Waters, Milford, MA) and monitored on a Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer (ThermoFisher Scientific, San Jose, CA).  Elution was performed over a 120 minute gradient at a rate of 400 nL/min with buffer B ranging from 3% to 80% (buffer A: 0.1% FA and 5% DMSO in water, buffer B: 0.1 % FA and 5% DMSO in ACN).  The mass spectrometer cycle was programmed to collect one full MS scan followed by 10 data dependent MS/MS scans.  The MS scans (300-1800 m/z range, 1,000,000 automatic gain control (AGC), 150 ms maximum ion time) were collected at a resolution of 70,000 at m/z 200 in profile mode, and the MS/MS spectra (2 m/z isolation width, 25% collision energy, 100,000 AGC target, 50 ms maximum ion time) were acquired at a resolution of 17,500 at m/z 200.  Dynamic exclusion was set to exclude previous sequenced precursor ions for 30 seconds within a 10 ppm window.  Precursor ions with +1 and +6 or higher charge states were excluded from sequencing.

###TMT Mass Spectrometry (ROSMAP)
All fractions were resuspended in an equal volume of loading buffer (0.1% FA, 0.03% TFA, 1% ACN) and analyzed by liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry essentially as described[11], with slight modifications. Peptide eluents were separated on a self-packed C18 (1.9 μm, Dr. Maisch, Germany) fused silica column (25 cm × 75 μM internal diameter (ID); New Objective, Woburn, MA) by a Dionex UltiMate 3000 RSLCnano liquid chromatography system (ThermoFisher Scientific) and monitored on an Orbitrap Fusion mass spectrometer (ThermoFisher Scientific). Sample elution was performed over a 180 min gradient with flow rate at 225 nL/min. The gradient was from 3% to 7% buffer B over 5 min, then 7% to 30% over 140 min, then 30% to 60% over 5 min, then 60% to 99% over 2 min, then held constant at 99% solvent B for 8 min, and then back to 1% B for an additional 20 min to equilibrate the column. The mass spectrometer was set to acquire in data dependent mode using the top speed workflow with a cycle time of 3 seconds. Each cycle consisted of 1 full scan followed by as many MS/MS (MS2) scans that could fit within the time window. The full scan (MS1) was performed with an m/z range of 350-1500 at 120,000 resolution (at 200 m/z) with AGC set at 4x10^5^, and maximum injection time 50 ms. The most intense ions were selected for higher energy collision-induced dissociation (HCD) at 38% collision energy with an isolation of 0.7 m/z, a resolution of 30,000, an AGC setting of 5x10^4, and a maximum injection time of 100 ms. Five of the 50 TMT batches (b01, b02, b03, b05, and b11) were run on the Orbitrap Fusion mass spectrometer using the SPS-MS3 method as previously described[9]. Batch b06 was has both MS2 and MS3 quantitation, but the data summarized here for this batch is based on MS2 only. 

###Label-free Quantification 
For the consensus LFQ search, 645 RAW files, including individual cases and pooled GIS samples from the MSSB, ACT, Banner and BLSA cohorts, were uploaded onto the Amazon Web Services (AWS) Cloud and analyzed using MaxQuant v1.6.3.4 with Thermo Foundation 2.0 for RAW file reading capability.  The Mayo, BLSA precuneus, Aging, and UPenn cohorts were each searched separately using MaxQuant.  The search engine Andromeda was used to build and search a concatenated target-decoy UniProt Knowledgebase (UniProtKB) containing both Swiss-Prot and TrEMBL human reference protein sequences (90,411 target sequences downloaded April 21, 2015), plus 245 contaminant proteins included as a parameter for the Andromeda search within MaxQuant[12].  Methionine oxidation (+15.9949 Da), asparagine and glutamine deamidation (+0.9840 Da), and protein N-terminal acetylation (+42.0106 Da) were variable modifications (up to 5 allowed per peptide); cysteine was assigned a fixed carbamidomethyl modification (+57.0215 Da).  Only fully tryptic peptides with up to 2 miscleavages were considered in the database search.  A precursor mass tolerance of ±20 ppm was applied prior to mass accuracy calibration, and ±4.5 ppm after internal MaxQuant calibration. Other search settings included a maximum peptide mass of 6,000 Da, a minimum peptide length of 6 residues, and 0.05 Da tolerance for high resolution MS/MS scans.  The false discovery rate (FDR) for peptide spectral matches, proteins, and site decoy fraction were each set to 1 percent.  Quantification settings were as follows: re-quantify with a second peak-finding attempt after protein identification is complete; match full MS1 peaks between runs; use a 0.7 min retention time match window after an alignment function was found with a 20 minute retention time search space.  The label free quantitation (LFQ) algorithm in MaxQuant[13, 14] was used for protein quantitation.  The quantitation method considered only razor and unique peptides for protein level quantitation.  The total summed protein intensity was also used to assess overall signal drift across samples prior to LFQ normalization.  Retention time internal standards were identified by searching against a small database containing the isotopic peptide standard sequences, keratins, and brain-specific spectrins with fixed modification of +8.014 Da (Lys) and +10.008 Da (Arg) using Proteome Discoverer 1.4.  Briefly, precursor mass tolerance was ±10 ppm, fragment ion tolerance was 0.05 Da, and FDR was enforced by Percolator[15] at 1%, enabling identification of MS/MS spectra for 14 of the 15 standard peptides.  Thermo .MSF files were imported as peptide searches into Skyline 3.1[16] with chromatograms within 2 minutes of an MS/MS match to one of the standard peptides.  Identified peak boundaries were visually checked and adjusted as necessary, and precursor (M, M+1, and M+2) isotopic peak areas were exported.  These areas were summed, and each peak area was divided by the average area of the corresponding peak across all runs to calculate aggregate signal responsiveness within the run.

###CSF Samples
All participants from whom CSF samples were collected provided informed consent under protocols approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at Emory University.  All patients received standardized cognitive assessments (including MoCA) in the Emory Cognitive Neurology clinic, the Emory Goizueta Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center (ADRC), and affiliated research studies (Emory Healthy Brain Study [EHBS] and Emory M2OVE-AD study).  All diagnostic data were supplied by the ADRC and the Emory Cognitive Neurology Program.  CSF was collected by lumbar puncture and banked according to 2014 ADC/NIA best practices guidelines.  For patients recruited from the Emory Cognitive Neurology Clinic, CSF samples were sent to Athena Diagnostics and assayed for Aβ42, total-Tau, and phospho-Tau (CSF ADmark®) using the INNOTEST® assay platform.  CSF samples collected from research participants in the ADRC, EHBS, and M2OVE-AD were assayed using the INNO-BIA AlzBio3 Luminex assay.  In total, there were two cohorts of CSF samples that were used in the proteomics studies.  Cohort 1 contained CSF samples from 150 healthy controls and 148 MCI/AD patients with full trait data.  Cohort 2 included CSF obtained from three groups:  32 cognitively normal, 31 AsymAD, and 33 MCI/AD.  Cases and normal individuals with AsymAD were defined using established biomarker cutoff criteria for AD for each assay platform[1, 2].
###CSF Protein Digestion
To generate peptides, all crude CSF samples were digested with LysC and trypsin.  Briefly, 20 µL CSF from each sample was reduced and alkylated with 0.4 µL 0.5 M tris-2(-carboxyethyl)-phosphine (TCEP) and 2 µL 0.4 M chloroacetamide (CAA) with heating at 90°C for 10 min, followed by a 15 min water bath sonication.  The samples were then further denatured by the addition of 67.2 µL of 8 M urea buffer (8 M urea, 100 mM NaHPO4, pH 8.5) and digested overnight with 1.9 µg LysC (Wako) (1:10 enzyme to protein ratio according to the highest amount of sample). Following LysC digestion, the samples were diluted to 1 M urea using 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate.  The same amount of trypsin (Promega) was then added (1:10 enzyme to protein ratio) and digestion was carried out for another 12 h.  After trypsin digestion, the peptide solutions were acidified with a 1% TFA and 10% FA solution to a final concentration of 0.1% TFA and 1% FA.  Peptides were desalted with a 30 mg C18 HLB column (Waters) and eluted in 1 mL of 50% ACN.  Aliquots (120 µL) from cohort 1 (n=298) or cohort 2 (n=96) samples were pooled together and split into equal volume aliquots (880 µL) for use as the global internal standard (GIS) for TMT labeling.  All samples and GIS were dried using a SpeedVac.
###TMT Boost Channel
Signals of low abundant proteins in the TMT 11-plex were amplified using a boost channel, as previously described[3, 4].  A pooled CSF sample was created separately for each cohort by combining 50 µL from each sample in cohort 1 or cohort 2 into a pool for each cohort.  Abundant proteins were removed using the High Select Top14 Abundant Proteins Depletion Resin (Thermo Scientific A36372BR) according to the manufacturer’s protocol, using a CSF-to-resin volume ratio of 1:1 and an incubation time of 15 min.  After immunodepletion, protein concentrations were determined by BCA.  Proteins were then reduced and alkylated (10 mM TCEP, 40 mM CAA) for 10 minutes at 90 °C.  The samples were then subjected to bath sonication for 15 min and dried under vacuum in a SpeedVac.  The immunodepleted pooled samples were re-suspended in 6 M urea buffer (6 M urea, 75 mM NaHPO4, pH 8.5) at half the volume of the pooled sample prior to evaporation.  Samples were digested overnight with LysC at an enzyme to protein ratio of 1:10.  The following day, samples were diluted with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate to reduce the urea concentration to 1M, and trypsin (Promega) was added (1:10 enzyme to protein ratio).  Digestion was allowed to proceed for 12 hr.  Peptides were then desalted using a 200 mg C18 Sep-Pak column, and the eluate was dried using a SpeedVac.  Aliquots (600 µg) of the immunodepleted pooled CSF samples were separately dissolved in 100 mM TEAB buffer (625 μL) and labeled with 5 mg of TMT 126 channel reagent (cohort 1 lot# TF266326, cohort 2 lot# SG253447, ThermoFisher Scientific) in anhydrous ACN (256 μL).  The reactions were allowed to proceed for 1 hr, and were subsequently quenched by adding 5% hydroxylamine (50 μL) and incubating for 15 min.  The 126 channel was then added to the other channels, as described below.
###TMT Labeling of Individual and GIS CSF Samples
All samples, including the GIS, were labeled with the 10-plex TMT kit plus an additional channel, for a total of 11 TMT channels (cohort 1 lot# TG273545 for 10-plex, TG273555 for channel 131C; cohort 2 lot# SI258088 for 10-plex, SJ258847 for channel 131C, ThermoFisher Scientific).  Samples were grouped into batches.  The TMT labeling kit was equilibrated to room temperature and dissolved in anhydrous ACN (256 μL).  The samples were reconstituted in 100 mM TEAB buffer (50 μL) and mixed with 0.4 mg (20.5 μL) of the corresponding labeling reagent.  The labeling reactions were allowed to proceed for 1 hr, and were subsequently quenched with 5% hydroxylamine (4 μL).  Per each TMT batch, labeled peptides from 9 channels (127N, 128N, 128C, 129N, 129C, 130N, 130C, 131, 131C) were mixed, desalted using a 100 mg C18 Sep-Pak column, and dried using a SpeedVac.  The immunodepleted pooled sample labeled with the 126 channel (boost channel) was then added to each 9-channel TMT mixture at a ratio of 50:1 pooled to individual CSF sample by original volume:volume prior to evaporation.  The sample mixtures were desalted using a 200 mg C18 Sep-Pak column, and dried using a SpeedVac. 
###Mass Spectrometry Analysis of CSF 
All samples were resuspended in equal volume of loading buffer (0.1% FA, 0.03% TFA, 1% ACN).  Peptide eluents were separated on a self-packed C18 (1.9 µm, Dr. Maisch, Germany) fused silica column (25 cm × 75 μM internal diameter (ID): New Objective, Woburn, MA) by an Easy-nLC system (ThermoFisher Scientific) and monitored on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (ThermoFisher Scientific) interfaced with a high-field asymmetric waveform ion mobility spectrometry (FAIMS) Pro.  Sample elution was performed over a 180 min gradient (buffer A: 0.1% FA in water, buffer B: 0.1% FA in 80% ACN) with flow rate at 225 nL/min.  The gradient was from 1% to 8% buffer B over 3 min, then from 8% to 40% over 160 min, then from 40% to 99% over 10 min, and then held at 99% B for 10 min. The mass spectrometer was set to acquire data in positive ion mode using data dependent acquisition and three (-50, -65 and -85 V) different compensation voltages (CV)[5].  Data were acquired at each CV for 1 s during each cycle.  Each cycle consisted of 1 full scan followed by as many MS2 and MS3 scans as possible within a 1 s timeframe. The full scan was performed with an m/z range of 450-1500 at 120,000 resolution (at 200 m/z) with an AGC setting of 4x105 and maximum injection time 50 ms.  The collision induced dissociation (CID) MS/MS scans were collected in the ion trap with an isolation window of 0.7 m/z, a collision energy of 35%, AGC setting of 1x104, and a maximum injection time of 50 ms.  The top 10 product ions were subjected to HCD synchronous precursor selection-based MS3 (SPS-MS3) as previously described[6].  For SPS-MS3 scans the isolation window was set to 2 m/z, the resolution to 50,000, the AGC to 1x105, and the maximum injection time to 105 ms.  For both cohorts, a single preliminary run of TMT batch 1 using the above parameters was used to create a target inclusion list of peptides that specifically excluded those from the top 15 most abundant proteins.  This inclusion list was used for all TMT batches in cohort 1 (n=38) and in cohort 2 (n=12).
###Database Searches and Protein Quantification of CSF 
All RAW files were analyzed using the Proteome Discoverer Suite (version 2.3, ThermoFisher Scientific).  MS/MS spectra were searched against the UniProtKB human proteome database (downloaded April 2015 with 90,411 total sequences).  The Sequest HT search engine was used to search the RAW files, with search parameters specified as follows:  fully tryptic specificity, maximum of two missed cleavages, minimum peptide length of 6, fixed modifications for TMT tags on lysine residues and peptide N-termini (+229.162932 Da) and carbamidomethylation of cysteine residues (+57.02146 Da), variable modifications for oxidation of methionine residues (+15.99492 Da), serine, threonine and tyrosine phosphorylation (+79.966 Da) and deamidation of asparagine and glutamine (+0.984 Da), precursor mass tolerance of 20 ppm, and a fragment mass tolerance of 0.6 Da.  Percolator was used to filter PSMs and peptides to an FDR of less than 1%.  Following spectral assignment, peptides were assembled into proteins and were further filtered based on the combined probabilities of their constituent peptides to a final FDR of 1%.  In cases of redundancy, shared peptides were assigned to the protein sequence in adherence with the principles of parsimony.  Reporter ions were quantified from MS3 scans using an integration tolerance of 20 ppm with the most confident centroid setting, as previously described[6].  Cohort 1 search and quantification results are available at DOI: 10.7303/syn21445083, and Cohort 2 search and quantification results are available at DOI: 10.7303/syn21445079.

Next-Generation Preclinical Models of NF1 Brain Tumours
# Next-Generation Preclinical Models of NF1 Brain Tumours
## GFF - Next Generation Models
### Principal Investigator: Jürgen A. Knoblich, PhD
### Project Lead / Data Coordinator: Jürgen A. Knoblich, PhD
### Institution: IMBA - Institute of Molecular Biotechnology
### Project Description:
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a genetic condition caused by mutations in the NF1 tumor suppressor gene (TSG). Individuals with NF1 are prone to the development of benign and malignant tumors, particularly brain and nerve tumors. One of the most common of these tumors is the low-grade glioma (optic pathway glioma; OPG), which can be associated with vision loss or early onset puberty. While mouse Nf1-OPG models have been developed, they do not lend themselves well to rapid drug discovery and evaluation. For this reason, we aim to employ human cerebral organoids to develop tissue culture models of NF1-associated low grade gliomas (LGGs). Cerebral organoids represent a groundbreaking 3D culture system, initially developed in the Knoblich laboratory, which accurately models human-specific aspects of brain development. To establish next-generation tissue culture models of human NF1-LGG, specifically NF1-OPG, we propose to generate cerebral organoids, including models where the timing of NF1 loss can be monitored, as well as assembloids, which better represent human NF1-OPGs. The simplicity of this system will allow us to study the impact of NF1 mutation on brain tumor development. This proposed project has the potential to generate more accurate human models of NF1-associated LGGs amenable to rapid drug screening.

hits.description:
**Data description **

**RNA extraction and library preparation**  

Parietal lobe tissue of post-mortem brain was obtained with informed consent for research use and were approved by Washington University in St. Louis review board. RNA was extracted from frozen brain using Tissue Lyser LT and RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). RNA-seq was generated for 19 brains from The Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network (DIAN), 84 brains with late-onset AD and 16 non-demented controls from The Charles F. and Joanne Knight Alzheimer's Disease Research Center (Knight ADRC) [1]. CDR scores were obtained during regular visits throughout the study prior to the subject’s decease [2]. A range of other pathological measurement were collected during autopsy including Braak staging, as previously described [3].  

RNA was extracted from frozen brain tissues using Tissue Lyser LT and RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) following the manufacturer’s instruction. RIN (RNA integrity) and DV200 were measured with RNA 6000 Pico Assay using Bioanalyzer 2100 (Agilent Technologies). The RIN is determined by the software on the Bioanalyzer taking into account the entire electrophoretic trace of the RNA including the presence or absence of degradation products. The DV200 value is defined as the percentage of nucleotides greater than 200nt. RIN and DV200 for all the samples can be found on Additional file 1: Table S1 [4]. The yield of each sample is determined by the Quant-iT RNA Assay (Life Technologies) on the Qubit Fluorometer (Fisher Scientific). The cDNA library was prepared with the TruSeq Stranded Total RNA Sample Prep with Ribo-Zero Gold kit (Illumina) and then sequenced by HiSeq 4000 (Illumina) using 2×150 paired end reads at McDonnell Genome Institute, Washington University in St. Louis with a mean of 58.14 ± 8.62 million reads. Number of reads and other QC metrics can be found in Additional file 1: Table S1 [4]. 

**RNA-seq QC and Alignment **

FastQC was applied to DIAN and Knight-ADRC RNAseq data to perform quality check on various aspects of sequencing quality [5]. The DIAN and Knight-ADRC dataset was aligned to human GRCh37 primary assembly using Star (ver 2.5.2b) [6]. We used the primary assembly and aligned reads to the assembled chromosomes, un-localized and unplaced scaffolds, and discarded alternative haploid sequences. Sequencing metrics, including coverage, distribution of reads in the genome [7], ribosomal and mitochondrial contents and alignment quality, were further obtained by applying Picard CollectRnaSeqMetrics (ver 2.8.2) to detect sample deviation. Additional QC metrics can be found in Additional file 1: Table S1 [4]. 

Aligned and sorted  bam files were loaded into IGV [8] to perform visual inspection of target variants. Samples carrying unexpected variants or missing expected variants were labeled as potential swapped samples. In addition, variants were called from RNA-seq following BWA/GATK pipeline [9, 10]. The identity of the samples was later verified by performing IBD analysis against genomic typing from GWAS chipsets.  

**Expression quantification **

We applied Salmon transcript expression quantification (ver 0.7.2) [11] to infer the gene expression for all samples included in the reference panel and participants in the Mayo, MSBB, DIAN and Knight-ADRC. We quantified the coding transcripts of Homo Sapiens included in the GENCODE reference genome (GRCh37.75).  

 

**Reference **

2.Morris JC: Clinical dementia rating: a reliable and valid diagnostic and staging measure for dementia of the Alzheimer type. Int Psychogeriatr 1997, 9 Suppl 1:173-176; discussion 177-178. 

3.Braak H, Braak E: Staging of Alzheimer's disease-related neurofibrillary changes. Neurobiol Aging 1995, 16:271-278; discussion 278-284. 

4.Li Z, Del-Aguila JL, Dube U, Budde J, Martinez R, Black K, Xiao Q, Cairns NJ, Dougherty JD, Lee JM, et al: Genetic variants associated with Alzheimer's disease confer different cerebral cortex cell-type population structure. Genome Med 2018, 10:43. 

5.S. A: FastQC: a quality control tool for high throughput sequence data. 2010. 

6.Dobin A, Davis CA, Schlesinger F, Drenkow J, Zaleski C, Jha S, Batut P, Chaisson M, Gingeras TR: STAR: ultrafast universal RNA-seq aligner. Bioinformatics 2013, 29:15-21. 

7.Broad Institute The Picard Pipeline [http://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/] 

8.Robinson JT, Thorvaldsdottir H, Winckler W, Guttman M, Lander ES, Getz G, Mesirov JP: Integrative genomics viewer. Nat Biotechnol 2011, 29:24-26. 

9.Li H, Durbin R: Fast and accurate short read alignment with Burrows-Wheeler transform. Bioinformatics 2009, 25:1754-1760. 

10.McKenna A, Hanna M, Banks E, Sivachenko A, Cibulskis K, Kernytsky A, Garimella K, Altshuler D, Gabriel S, Daly M, DePristo MA: The Genome Analysis Toolkit: a MapReduce framework for analyzing next-generation DNA sequencing data. Genome Res 2010, 20:1297-1303.

# Data Sharing for Wingo et al. *The role of sex in brain protein expression and disease*

## Methods

Please see methods in Wingo et al. *The role of sex in brain protein expression and disease* for complete methods and data description. In brief, genotyping was filtered to sites present in the [LDRef Panel](https://data.broadinstitute.org/alkesgroup/FUSION/LDREF.tar.bz2) and combined with brain transcript and protein expression data using [FUSION](http://gusevlab.org/projects/fusion) to generate brain protein weights. # Brain Tumor Progression Challenge {row} {column width=2} {column} {column width=4} #### ${jointeam?teamId=3495691&isChallenge=true&isMemberMessage=You have successfully joined the challenge&text=Click here to join!&isSimpleRequestButton=true&requestOpenText=Your registration is in progress&successMessage=Your registration is in progress} {column} {column width=5} ###! There are ${teammembercount?teamId=3495691} registered participants.
**Join them now!** {column} {column width=1} {column} {row} --- ## Overview Brain tumors are among the most researched diseases in the field of medical image computing. This is also reflected by the popularity of challenges like the [MICCAI2024 BraTS Challenge](https://www.synapse.org/BraTS2024), the [MICCAI2024 FeTS Challenge](https://www.synapse.org/FeTS2024), and the use of brain MRIs in challenges like [MICCAI2024 MOOD Challenge](https://www.synapse.org/MOOD) for anomaly detection. Most research, however, focuses only on single time-points, even when evaluating longitudinal properties like disease progression. We address this significant gap in current research with the **MICCAI2024 Brain Tumor Progression Challenge (BraTPRO)**. The goal of this challenge is the development of methods for the **classification** of response according to the RANO criteria from longitudinal brain tumor MRIs. RANO distinguishes four types of response between consecutive images, namely complete response, partial response, stable disease and progressive disease. During training, ground truth segmentation masks are available as additional supervision signal. The challenge is split in two tasks. In the first task, the focus is on method development for which we provide a development dataset. Submitted methods will subsequently be trained and evaluated on hidden train and test sets. For the second task, participants are free to train their models with all data available - public as well as private - and submit the trained models only for evaluation on the hidden test set. The detailed challenge description can be found on [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/10991975) For more information also check out [Github](https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/BraTPRO). --- ## Timeline All dates are subject to change, also check the Announcements! | --**1. April**-- | - --Challenge launch-- | | --**16 August**-- | - --Opening of evaluation pipeline for validation-- | | --**18.August**-- | - --Opening of evaluation pipeline for final submission-- | | **10. September 23:59 GMT+2** | - Validation docker submission deadline | | **13. September 23:59 GMT+2** | - Final docker submission deadline | | **15. September 23:59 GMT+2** | - Short paper submission deadline
- Deadline to open source submitted algorithm | Announcements 22\. August 2024: Challenge submissions recently opened. For more information check the [latest update](https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn53752772/discussion/threadId=11538). 11\. August 2024: Challenge submissions will finally open in the next two days and the submission deadline is extended until 10th of September. Check the [Update on Challenge Submissions](https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn53752772/discussion/threadId=11473) post for more info. Data Information about the datasets used in this challenge, as well as the employed dataset structure for training and inference can be found in the respective subpages: [Dataset Structure](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn53752772/wiki/627324) [Development Dataset](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn53752772/wiki/627322) [Train and Test Dataset](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn53752772/wiki/627323) Evaluation Following the guidelines from the Metrics Reloaded Framework [1], all submissions will be evaluated using **Balanced Accuracy (BA), F1-score, True Positive Rate (TPR), True Negative Rate (TNR), Average Precision (AP), and Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC)**. Submissions will be ranked using the average ranks of **F1-score** and **AP** per class and metrics. Evaluation code is available on [Github](https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/BraTPRO/blob/master/evaluation/metrics.py). References: [1] Maier-Hein, L., Reinke, A. et al. "Metrics reloaded: recommendations for image analysis validation" Nature methods 21, 1-18 (2024), ArXiv:2206.01653 How To Participate The following subpages list the requirements for submitted models, instructions for docker submission and short paper submission: [Model Requirements](https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn53752772/wiki/627325) [Docker Submission](https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn53752772/wiki/627319) [Short Paper Submission](https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn53752772/wiki/627321) Organizers Yannick Kirchhoff, Tassilo Wald, Balint Kovacs, Maximilian Zenk, Klaus Maier-Hein _German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), Heidelberg, Division of Medical Image Computing, Germany_ Philipp Vollmuth _German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), Heidelberg, Division of Medical Image Computing, Germany_ _Department of Neuroradiology, Heidelberg University Hospital, Germany_ _Division for Computational Radiology Clinical AI (CCIBonn.ai), Clinic for Neuroradiology, University Hospital Bonn, Bonn, Germany_ Jens Kleesiek, Jan Egger _Institute for AI in Medicine (IKIM), University Hospital Essen, Germany_ Yannick Suter, Mauricio Reyes _ARTORG Center, University Bern, Switzerland_ André Ferreira _Center Algoritmi, University of Minho, Braga, Portugal_ _Institute for AI in Medicine (IKIM), University Hospital Essen, Germany_ Spyridon Bakas, _Indiana University, Indianapolis, IN, USA_ Raymond Y Huang, _MGB, Boston, MA, USA_ Javier Villanueva-Meyer, _University of California San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA_ _AI-RANO Group leads_ Rules We expect participants to follow best scientific practices. In case of any suspected misconduct of violation of the specific rules defined below, we reserve the right to exclude participants from the challenge, as well as any follow-up publications. - No pretraining is allowed in task 1. Models must be trained completely from scratch - Teams are allowed one submission for final evaluation for task 1 and 2, respectively - We will be able to support O(50) submissions for model training in task 1. In case of too many submissions, we will only evaluate submissions from the best performing teams in task 2. - The top 3 performing methods for both tasks will be announced publicly at the conference if they don't opt-out and the teams will be invited to present their methods - All teams are free to decide if they want to show up on the public leaderboard - Teams will be invited to nominate members as co-authors of the challenge follow-up publication if they: - follow all the rules - open-source their algorithm - hand in a short paper describing their method - All submissions will be used for the final publication, irrespective of whether the teams decide to nominate co-authors or show up on the leaderboard - Teams are encouraged to publish their methods separately and we will not enforce an embargo time. - We hope that we will be able to award prizes, eligibility for prizes requires that participants: - follow all the rules - open-source their algorithm - hand in a short paper describing their method Tasks This challenge consists of two tasks, both tackling the classification of response in longitudinal brain tumor MRI according to the RANO criteria [1] - complete response, partial response, stable disease, and progressive disease. The tasks are detailed below: ### Task 1: RANO Classifier Development In this task, participants need to develop methods for the classification of RANO criteria, which will be submitted for training and evaluation on the organizer's computing infrastructure. This task represents an idealized setting where training and test set are iid. The focus of this task is therefore on methodological improvements. We recommend using the provided [development dataset](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn53752772/wiki/627322). ### Task 2: Data-driven RANO classification In this task, participants will train their developed methods for the classification of RANO criteria on all data available to them - public as well as private data sources. Trained models will be submitted as docker images to be evaluated on the hidden test set. This task is therefore set in a more realistic setting as one would encounter in a real clinical environment. References: [1] Wen PY, Macdonald DR, Reardon DA, et al. "Updated response assessment criteria for high-grade gliomas: Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology Working Group." Journal of Clinical Oncology 28:1963-1972 (2010) Docker Submission Submissions to this challenge are done in the form of [Docker](https://www.docker.com/get-started) containers, which are then executed on our local infrastructure. We recommend building your Docker container using a suitable base image, depending on if you use [PyTorch](https://hub.docker.com/r/pytorch/pytorch/), [TensorFlow](https://www.tensorflow.org/install/docker) or some other deep learning framework. ### Docker setup Your docker needs to have the following scripts, which will be run during evaluation. #### Task 1 ` /workspace/run_training.sh train_data_dir checkpoint_dir ` for training on the private training set ` /workspace/run_inference.sh checkpoint_dir test_data_dir pred_dir ` for testing on the private test set The following docker commands will be given: ``` docker run --gpus all -v "train_data_dir/:/mnt/train_data" -v "checkpoint_dir:/mnt/checkpoint" --read-only docker-image-name /workspace/run_training.sh /mnt/train_data /mnt/checkpoint docker run --gpus all -v "checkpoint_dir/:/mnt/checkpoint" -v "test_data_dir:/mnt/test_data" -v "pred_dir:/mnt/pred" --read-only docker-image-name /workspace/run_inference.sh /mnt/checkpoint /mnt/test_data /mnt/pred ``` #### Task 2 ` /workspace/run_inference.sh test_data_dir pred_dir ` for testing on the private test set The following docker commands will be given: ``` docker run --gpus all -v "test_data_dir:/mnt/test_data" -v "pred_dir:/mnt/pred" --read-only docker-image-name /workspace/run_inference.sh /mnt/checkpoint /mnt/test_data /mnt/pred ``` ### How to submit In order to submit your docker to the challenge you need to first create a project on synapse and give it a meaningful name (this is not required but advised). This project will have a **unique** Project ID (e.g. syn12345678), which you will need in the following. After creating your docker image locally, you can upload it to the synapse docker registry ``` docker login docker.synapse.org docker tag docker_imagename docker.synapse.org/synapse_project_ID/docker_imagename docker push docker.synapse.org/synapse_project_ID/docker_imagename:latest ``` In order to submit the uploaded Docker image you need to: - go to your project -> Docker and choose the Docker image you want to submit - click on Docker Repository Tools -> Submit Docker Repository to Challenge - choose the correct tag and the evaluation queue you want to submit to - specify if you submit alone or as a team and finally click on submit Model Requirements Models should be able to read two images, either original or affinely registered to the respective baseline images, and output class probabilities for the different response types. The mapping from response to class used in this challenge is given by: ``` 0: complete response 1: partial response 2: stable disease 3: progressive disease ``` During training, ground truth segmentation masks are available as additional supervision signal. The model should be able to read the patients.json file as detailed in the [Dataset Structure](https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn53752772/wiki/627324) section. During inference models should output a predictions.json file, to be saved in the given directory, containing the predicted class probabilities for each case given in the patients.json file. The output should look like this: { "patient_01": { "case_1": { "response": [0.8, 0.1, 0.1, 0] }, ... }, "patient_02": { "case_1": { "response": [0.04, 0.06, 0.75, 0.15] }, ... }, ... } #### Restrictions for Model Training For training in task 1 you will have access to a NVidia Titan RTX GPU with 24 GB of VRAM, 6 cores/12 threads and 64 GB RAM. Trainings may take a maximum of 24 hours, make sure to save frequently save checkpoints so you don't lose your training progress! During the validation phase, runs are limited to one hour and should be killed by the participants after the first few epochs. Keep in mind, that the GPUs are part of a node and therefore have shared resources. **Don't use multiprocessing.cpu_count() or similar but stick to the fix limits given here!** #### Restrictions for Model Testing Inference will is done on NVidia RTX 2080 GPUs with 11 GB of VRAM, 8 cores/16 threads and 64 GB RAM. There is a time limit per case of 10 minutes, which hopefully won't be a problem. This time limit is only enforced on the validation set in order to guarantee that each case will be predicted. Final submissions will be tested on the validation set to ensure they meet the limits! Short Paper Submission In addition to the docker submission, each participant is required to submit a short description of their respective solution. You can orientate yourself on the [DREAM Challenge Writeup Template](https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn2351771/wiki/62369) but don't have to follow it strictly. Your writeup should include: - Title of your submission - Author List - Short Introduction, this does **not** need to give a general overview but should be tailored towards your submission - Method section, describe what you did, this can go more in depth - Results section, either results from your own (cross-)validation or the validation phase - Conclusion/Discussion - References Wriiteups should be sent via mail to yannick.kirchhoff@dkfz-heidelberg.de. Dataset Structure We will use a specific dataset structure for training and inference, which we recommend to adapt, at least for the model development in task 1. This dataset structure is partially oriented on the nnUNet dataset structure. A script to convert the provided [development dataset](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn53752772/wiki/627322) to this dataset structure is also available on [Github](https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/BraTPRO/blob/master/dataset_download/download_and_convert_dataset.py). ### Dataset structure for training and testing: BraTPRO_Dataset/ ├── images │   ├── patient_01_scan_01 │   │   ├── patient_01_scan_01_0000.nii.gz │   │   ├── patient_01_scan_01_0001.nii.gz │   │   ├── patient_01_scan_01_0002.nii.gz │   │   ├── patient_01_scan_01_0003.nii.gz │   ├── patient_01_scan_02 │   ├── patient_01_scan_03 │   ├── patient_01_scan_04 │   ├── patient_02_scan_01 │   ├── patient_02_scan_02 │   ├── patient_02_scan_03 │   ├── ... ├── segmentations │   ├── patient_01_scan_01.nii.gz │   ├── patient_01_scan_02.nii.gz │   ├── ... ├── images_registered │   ├── patient_01_scan_01_reg │   ├── patient_01_scan_02_reg │   ├── patient_01_scan_03_reg │   ├── patient_01_scan_04_reg │   ├── patient_02_scan_01_reg │   ├── patient_02_scan_02_reg │   ├── patient_02_scan_03_reg │   ├── ... ├── segmentations_registered │   ├── patient_01_scan_01_reg.nii.gz │   ├── patient_01_scan_02_reg.nii.gz │   ├── ... ├── patients.json The **images** contains all original scans, while **images_registered** includes all scans affinely registered to the respective baseline scans. The different MRI sequences are indicated by the modality identifiers **000i**, where T1: 0, T1c: 1, T2: 2, FLAIR: 3. Segmentations are saved similarly to the images in the **segmentations** and **segmentations_registered** folders. The folder structure will be created by the conversion script; however, models only need to handle the **patients.json** for training and testing. This file contains all relevant information regarding the training cases, including patient identifiers, relative paths of scans (original and registered to the baseline) and response labels. Example content of **patients.json**: { "patient_01": { "case_1": { "baseline": "./images/patient_01_scan_01", "baseline_seg": "./segmentations/patient_01_scan_01.nii.gz", "baseline_registered": "./images_registered/patient_01_scan_01_reg", "baseline_seg_registered": "./segmentations_registered/patient_01_scan_01_reg.nii.gz", "followup": "./images/patient_01_scan_02", "followup_seg": "./segmentations/patient_01_scan_02.nii.gz", "followup_registered": "./images_registered/patient_01_scan_02_reg", "followup_seg_registered": "./segmentations_registered/patient_01_scan_02_reg.nii.gz", "response": 0 }, ... }, "patient_02": { "case_1": { "baseline": "./images/patient_02_scan_01", "baseline_seg": "./segmentations/patient_02_scan_01.nii.gz", "baseline_registered": "./images_registered/patient_02_scan_01_reg", "baseline_seg_registered": "./segmentations_registered/patient_02_scan_01_reg.nii.gz", "followup": "./images/patient_02_scan_02", "followup_seg": "./segmentations/patient_02_scan_02.nii.gz", "followup_registered": "./images_registered/patient_02_scan_02_reg", "followup_seg_registered": "./segmentations_registered/patient_02_scan_02_reg.nii.gz", "response": 2 }, ... }, ... } The mapping from response labels and the RANO responses in this challenge is given by: ``` 0: complete response 1: partial response 2: stable disease 3: progressive disease ``` Additionally, the labels in the segmentation files are given by: ``` 0: background 1: edema 2: contrast enhancing tumor ``` For inference the **patients.json** will only contain the test cases to be predicted. The "response" key and keys for the segmentations will not be present; models attempting to read these keys during inference will crash! Models should output a **predictions.json** file containing the predicted class probabilities as follows: { "patient_01": { "case_1": { "response": [0.8, 0.1, 0.1, 0] }, ... }, "patient_02": { "case_1": { "response": [0.04, 0.06, 0.75, 0.15] }, ... }, ... } Development Dataset The public [LUMIERE Dataset](https://springernature.figshare.com/collections/The_LUMIERE_Dataset_Longitudinal_Glioblastoma_MRI_with_Expert_RANO_Evaluation/5904905) [1] is provided for method development in Task 1 as well as model training in Task 2. It comprises 91 patients with a total of 616 scans and annotations according to RANO criteria. In addition to the RANO criteria, automatically generated segmentations by two deep learning tools, HD-GLIO-AUTO [2] and DeepBraTumIA [3], are also available. Follow this [link](https://springernature.figshare.com/articles/dataset/LUMIERE_dataset_-_MRI_data_and_automated_segmentations/21249516?backTo=/collections/The_LUMIERE_Dataset_Longitudinal_Glioblastoma_MRI_with_Expert_RANO_Evaluation/5904905) to download the MRI data and automatic segmentations and this [link](https://springernature.figshare.com/articles/dataset/LUMIERE_dataset_-_Expert_RANO_rating/21195556?backTo=/collections/The_LUMIERE_Dataset_Longitudinal_Glioblastoma_MRI_with_Expert_RANO_Evaluation/5904905) for the expert RANO ratings. A script to convert the downloaded dataset to the dataset structure as detailed [here](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn53752772/wiki/627324) is available at [Github](https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/BraTPRO/blob/master/dataset_download/download_and_convert_dataset.py). References: [1] Suter, Y., Knecht, U., Valenzuela, W., Notter, M., Hewer, E., Schucht, P., Wiest, R. and Reyes, M., 2022. "The LUMIERE dataset: Longitudinal Glioblastoma MRI with expert RANO evaluation." Scientific data, 9(1), p.768. [2] HD-GLIO-AUTO: https://github.com/CCI-Bonn/HD-GLIO-AUTO [3] DeepBraTumIA: https://www.nitrc.org/projects/deepbratumia/ Train and Test Dataset The hidden train and test set is a multi-centric dataset, previously used in [1], comprising 306 patients in total with annotations for RANO criteria, as well as ground truth segmentation masks. 200 patients will be used for training in task 1 and 100 patients as test set in task 1 and 2. The remaining 6 patients will be used for the validation phase. The train and test sets will be available in the dataset structure detailed [here](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn53752772/wiki/627324) for training and inference, respectively. References: [1] Kickingereder, P., Isensee, F. et al. "Automated quantitative tumor response assessment of MRI in neuro-oncology with artificial neural networks: a multicentre, retrospective study." The Lancet Oncology 20, 728-740 (2019) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1470-2045(19)30098-1
