hits.description:
${image?fileName=combinedLogo%5FwithTitle%2Epng&align=Center&responsive=true}

Metastasis remains the principal cause of mortality among cancer patients. For a tumor cell to metastasize, it must escape the primary tumor, successfully negotiate various molecular and cellular interactions, and colonize a new microenvironment to establish a secondary tumor. To predict how and when cancer will metastasize and to develop more effective treatments, a better understanding is needed about how these individual events - tumor growth, dissemination, colonization, and survival - contribute to the complex metastatic process. Recent advances in live-cell imaging, characterization of circulating tumor cells, experimental models of tumor dormancy, descriptions of tumor cell – immune system crosstalk, cell and tissue mechanics, and single-cell genomic and proteomic analysis have provided quantitative data that can be used to build testable mathematical and computational models of tumor metastasis. 
 
The Interdisciplinary Approaches to Cancer Metastasis workshop, to be held **June 12-14, 2017**, in Seattle, WA at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center, will bring together ~25 early stage investigators (within 15 years of terminal degree) across four NCI-supported programs, the Innovative Molecular Analysis Technologies ([IMAT](https://imat.cancer.gov)) program, the Informatics Technology for Cancer Research ([ITCR](https://itcr.nci.nih.gov)) program, the Cancer Systems Biology Consortium ([CSBC](http://csbconsortium.org)) and the Physical Sciences-Oncology Network ([PS-ON](https://physics.cancer.gov)), along with select outside investigators to tackle important questions in cancer metastasis. The goal is to form teams that utilize the technologies and computational approaches championed by IMAT and ITCR along with the cancer systems biology and physical oncology viewpoints employed within the CSBC and PS-ON. Teams will nucleate around a question in cancer metastasis that can best be addressed through an interdisciplinary approach.
 
Discussions at the workshop will be guided by distinguished scientist “[Mentors](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/wiki/408136),” who will assist in articulating project ideas and facilitate participant discussions both before and during the workshop. Select proposals developed during the Interdisciplinary Approaches to Cancer Metastasis workshop will be selected for funding through a process involving workshop participants, scientific Mentors, and NCI Program Staff. Specific details about the workshop can be found [here](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/wiki/408139).

<!--##Application details can be found [here](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/wiki/408137).-->



About the workshop
The IACM workshop is designed to solicit novel pilot project ideas and distribute funds to one or more **teams** of scientists from diverse institutions and backgrounds.  The workshop itself is divided into three stages, as preparation is required of the attendees before the workshop and follow-up is expected from those attendees who receive the pilot project funds.

###Pre-workshop activities
Ahead of the workshop selected applicants will meet weekly ~6 times to discuss ideas with other attendees and describe ideas via teleconference.  All applicants will gain access to [this Synapse project site](syn7433743) to facilitate discussions and brainstorming in between the meetings and ultimately form teams surrounding select ideas. Selected applicants are expected to:
* Register for a [Synapse account](http://www.synapse.org/register) to gain access
* Attend 6 weekly [virtual meetings](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn9693597) with the other selected attendees and selected mentors
* Initiate discussions in the [discussion forum](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/discussion/default) to identify other candidates to form teams
* Work with those teams begin to discuss project ideas and proposals

###Workshop agenda
Selected applicants are invited to Seattle, WA to participate in the workshop June 12-14, 2017.  This will give the attendees the ability to meet their teammates in person and solidify the project proposal with respect to the pilot project funds. Each team will arrive ready to present their ideas to the group and then refine these ideas and establish a budget throughout the workshop. At the end of the workshop each team will present their proposal to use some or all of the pilot project funds (~\$500,000 in total funds). 
 
All workshop attendees will rank the project proposals and the mentors and meeting organizers will use these rankings to select a final division of funds. Depending on the rankings and proposals, all funds may go to a single collaborative team or be divided among multiple teams. 

A more detailed agenda has been posted on the [IACM attendee page](syn9874222).

###Post-workshop followup
The team(s) selected to receive the pilot project funds will be given 1 year to carry out the research as well as modest travel funds to meet amongst themselves and/or present their ideas. 
Attendee Requirements
This page describes the pre-workshop activities required by invited attendees to the workshop. The goal of these activities is to facilitate the formation of teams that will be ready to kick-off the workshop with a brief presentation of their proposal, which will then be refined over the two-day workshop.
 
Below are the basic steps to get started: 

###Accessing data portal
This [Synapse Project](http://docs.synapse.org/articles/making_a_project.html) will provide ongoing updates for the workshop as we proceed through the planning activities.  You will require access to the full capabilities of this site to participate in [discussions](http://docs.synapse.org/articles/discussion.html) and make use of the [file sharing capabilities](http://docs.synapse.org/articles/versioning.html).  Specifically you will need to:
* Register for Synapse at http://www.synapse.org/register
* Log into synapse using your registered account (make sure you use your first and last name)
* Join the IACM workshop attendee team by clicking the button below:
${jointeam?teamId=3350418&isChallenge=false&isSimpleRequestButton=true&isMemberMessage=Already a member&successMessage=Successfully joined&text=Join&requestOpenText=Your request to join this team has been sent%2E}

This should provide you with edit capabilities to this site so you can [view the attendee information page](syn8568463) create folders and upload files, as well as join the discussions.

###Get to know other attendees
All attendee information has been posted to a [restricted site](syn8568463) that you can view once you have logged in.  Here we have more details about who will be attending the meeting and your responsibilities.

###Initiate discussions
We recommend you navigate to the [IACM Discussion Forum](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/discussion/default) to describe your project ideas and seek out new team members. The workshop organizers will post a few topic-based threads to get initial conversations started.

###Create team workspace
You can then begin to create folders under the [IACM Project Workspace](syn8063299) folder. Workshop organizers ask that you keep these folders and data available to all workshop attendees while teams are being formed, after which you can create your own synapse projects or private folders to continue planning.

###Teleconference to further discuss ideas
The workshop organizers will host numerous teleconferences that will provide a space for workshop attendees to discuss their ideas with potential team mates as well as workshop organizers.  Links to the teleconferences can be provided [here](syn9693597). 

###Prepare for workshop presentation
The workshop will kick off with presentations from all teams. More details forthcoming.
Workshop Application Process
###Workshop application period is now over. 

The workshop is primarily geared toward early stage investigators, designated as those that are within 15 years of a terminal degree*, who are interested in meeting new collaborators and expanding their current research portfolio. Those investigators that do not yet hold an independent position (i.e. postdoctoral fellow or research scientist) are welcome to apply, although if they are not recognized as Principal Investigators by their Institution they likely will not be eligible to receive pilot project funding.Workshop capacity is set at ~25 attendees, who will be selected from the pool of applicants by the NCI representatives, Sage Bionetworks and the [workshop mentors](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/wiki/408136). 

  

To apply to attend the workshop [download the application from here](http://csbconsortium.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/InterdisciplinaryWorkshopinCancerMetasasisApplication_final.docx) and send the completed application to iacmWorkshop@sagebase.org before the **February 15, 2017** deadline.

####Please direct any questions about the workshop or application process to iacmWorkshop@sagebase.org 

 *Exceptions to the ESI status will be considered on a case-by-case basis, please email iacmWorkshop@sagebase.org to inquire.
Workshop Mentors
We invited three mentors from the field of cancer metastasis to guide the workshop from inception to the final decisions.  Specifically these mentors:
* Helped select 25 investigators to invite to the workshop from the larger pool of applicants
* Directed researchers in the pre-workshop activities to focus on relevant themes
* Worked with teams to formulate cohesive proposals
* Advised organizing committee to select final project proposals to be funded

# Mechanisms of MPNST Metastasis
## CTF - Young Investigator Award
### Principal Investigator: Alexa Sheehan
### Project Lead / Data Coordinator: Alexa Sheehan
### Institution: University of Iowa
### Project Description:
Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs) are aggressive, highly metastatic sarcomas with poor clinical prognoses. Treatment of this cancer, especially when it metastasizes, has not improved over the last 30 years. Therefore, there is a critical need to further understand and target key aspects of MPNST progression to develop effective treatment options. The overall goal of this study is to identify and disrupt mechanisms of MPNST metastasis using novel therapeutics to ultimately improve outcomes for patients. We will utilize recently developed pharmaceutical agents to determine if inhibiting the function of lysyl oxidase enzymes can decrease MPNST metastasis. Lysyl oxidases (Lox) are proteins that modify the extracellular environment of tumor cells. Recently, we demonstrated that the expression of Loxs increases in MPNST cells that have loss-of-function mutations in the genetic regulator PRC2. Loss of PRC2 is also associated with increased metastasis in both mouse models and patients and we have determined that inhibiting Lox activity can significantly restrict this process (PMID 36066973). In this study, we will assess the ability of newer formulations of Lox inhibitors to decrease MPNST metastasis in our preclinical models. These next-generation agents are more specific and less toxic than previous versions and are currently being tested in clinical trials for fibrotic disease and some cancer types. We predict that these therapeutics will inhibit MPNST metastasis and could represent a promising treatment option for patients. Additionally, PRC2 loss is associated with global reprogramming of gene expression in MPNST. These changes result in increased expression of proteins that promote tumor growth, however they also induce instability which makes cells more sensitive to certain drugs that further enhance this state. These drugs, known as epigenetic modulators, inhibit growth of MPNST cells in vitro but have not been tested for their effects on metastasis. In this study, we will treat PRC2-deleted cells with a variety of these agents to determine their impact on cellular invasion and metastatic capabilities. We hypothesize that these modulators will restrict metastasis by decreasing expression of Lox enzymes. If this relationship is observed, will with combine epigenetic therapy with next-generation Lox inhibitors to assess if this further inhibits MPNST metastasis. Overall, we will use a variety of preclinical models to determine if increased Lox expression induced by PRC2 loss is a targetable treatment option for patients with metastatic MPNST.

hits.description:
**Tumorigenesis and Metastasis Analysis**

**Overview**

[Tumorigenesis and Metastasis Analysis](https://www.alfacytology.com/3d-cancer-models/tumorigenesis-and-metastasis-analysis.html) is a fundamental area of cancer research dedicated to understanding the biological mechanisms that drive tumor initiation, progression, invasion, and metastatic dissemination. Tumorigenesis involves the transformation of normal cells into malignant cells through the accumulation of genetic, epigenetic, and microenvironmental alterations, while metastasis represents the spread of cancer cells from the primary tumor to distant organs. Together, these processes are responsible for the majority of cancer-related mortality and remain central topics in oncology research.

This resource provides an overview of research approaches for investigating tumorigenesis and metastasis using advanced three-dimensional tumor models and integrated biological analyses. By combining physiologically relevant experimental systems with molecular, cellular, and functional characterization, researchers can better understand the mechanisms governing tumor development, metastatic progression, and therapeutic response, supporting both basic cancer research and translational oncology studies.

**Research Focus**

Tumorigenesis and Metastasis Analysis encompasses the investigation of multiple biological processes associated with cancer progression, including uncontrolled cell proliferation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), tumor cell migration, invasion, metastatic colonization, and interactions within the tumor microenvironment. Research also explores how genetic alterations, signaling pathways, extracellular matrix remodeling, immune regulation, angiogenesis, and stromal components collectively contribute to tumor progression and metastatic potential.

Studies may further examine the roles of cancer stem cells, tumor heterogeneity, cell-cell communication, and molecular biomarkers associated with metastatic disease. Integrating three-dimensional tumor models with imaging technologies, molecular profiling, and functional assays enables researchers to characterize the dynamic events involved in tumor initiation and metastasis while identifying potential therapeutic targets and predictive biomarkers for cancer treatment.

**Applications**

Tumorigenesis and Metastasis Analysis supports a broad range of oncology research applications, including cancer biology, metastasis research, tumor microenvironment characterization, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) studies, biomarker discovery, drug target validation, mechanism-of-action studies, precision oncology, and preclinical drug development. These research approaches also facilitate investigations into metastatic mechanisms, tumor invasion, therapeutic resistance, and the evaluation of novel anticancer therapies.

As research into tumor initiation and metastatic progression continues to evolve, physiologically relevant experimental models have become increasingly valuable for reproducing complex tumor biology and disease progression. Comprehensive tumorigenesis and metastasis analysis provides researchers with more predictive experimental systems for translational cancer research and contributes to the discovery of innovative therapeutic strategies aimed at preventing cancer progression and metastatic spread.

closeread HTAN outputs
# closeread: HTAN grounded publication extraction — outputs

This project holds the outputs of **closeread**, a pipeline that reads the full
text of HTAN (Human Tumor Atlas Network) publications and the papers that cite
them, and extracts structured, evidence-linked facts about how the atlases were
built and how their data was reused. **Every extracted fact is tied to a
verbatim quotation with character offsets in the source document.** Regular
expressions only locate text; a model decides meaning, and a second model
judges it.

Code: https://github.com/Sage-Bionetworks/closeread

## What was measured (snapshot 2026-08-21)

- 168 HTAN corpus publications (157 with full text)
- 9,753 deduplicated citing publications (6,072 with full text, including 626
  bioRxiv/medRxiv preprints recovered from the requester-pays source buckets)
- 12,524 citation edges; preprint/published pairs collapsed
- ~128,000 quotation-grounded records across 9 extraction classes

## Folder guide

| Folder | Contents |
|---|---|
| `metadata` | `documents.jsonl` (both corpora, with author-overlap classification), `citation_edges.jsonl`, `candidates.jsonl` (regex matches; locate text, never decide meaning), `vocab_map.jsonl` (model-generated canonicalisation), `model_gap_500_sample.json` (small-vs-strong model comparison) |
| `silver` | One JSONL per extraction run: judged, canonicalised records. **Contains superseded runs too** (nothing is deleted): filter by `metadata/REPORTED_RUNS.json`, or use `gold`, which is already filtered. Raw attribute values and canonical values sit side by side; judge verdicts attached; nothing deleted |
| `gold` | One flat CSV per extraction class — opens in Excel, loads in R with one line |
| `report` | `REPORT.md` (all numbers computed from records at render time) and `figure_manifest.json` (per-figure provenance: runs, record counts, denominators, filters) |
| `figures` | Eight figures (SVG + PNG), each with a CSV of exactly the plotted data |
| `runs` | Per-run summaries: model, token counts, finish reasons, alignment and attribute-population rates. Also the three `htan_provenance_20260821_00*.handoff.json` files: the document index for each provenance run, read by the HTAN DCC personas analysis |

## Reading the numbers honestly

- Every share carries its denominator; every reuse aggregate is split by
  author overlap (consortium-internal vs external).
- Precision is measured against 200 human-labelled records (`metadata/gold_labels.jsonl`): judge precision 93.0% and recall 95.6%; extraction precision 97.3% (data_acquisition) and 85.7% (engagement). Figure F8 states coverage and measured precision per class.
- The most frequent extraction error, from the labelling notes: a citing paper's own data-availability statement misread as data reuse (distribution mistaken for reuse). Read `data_reuse` counts with that bias in mind.
- The citing-side full-text passes ran on the small model. A 500-document
  strong-model sample (`metadata/model_gap_500_sample.json`) measured that the
  small model recovers only 42–62% of strong-model records on several classes
  — read citing-side counts as floors, not totals.
- Documents with no availability statement carry an explicit `no_statement`
  record; absence is recorded, never implied.

## Provenance

Extraction: Gemini batch API, temperature 0, canary-gated fan-outs. All
reported results come from the strong model (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`); the
small model (`gemini-3.1-flash-lite`) contributes only the corpus union, and
its citing runs were superseded after a judged sample measured 14-38%
record-level false positives (see `metadata/small_model_citing_judged_sample.json`). Sources:
OpenAlex (metadata, citation graph), PubMed Central OA bucket and
bioRxiv/medRxiv source buckets (full text), PubMed/Crossref (abstract
backfill). Total extraction cost 1,236 USD at batch rates, of which 701 USD was model reasoning (thinking) tokens billed as output; about 1,015 USD corresponds to the reported runs.

Contact: Ashley Clayton (@ashley.clayton), Sage Bionetworks.

- Canonical vocabulary state: assay_name and platform are second-pass consolidated (some near-duplicate canonicals survive; platform folds some instrument models together); other value sets are first-pass only. Do not read canonical counts as counts of distinct real-world entities.

hits.description:
${image?fileName=combinedLogo%5FwithTitle%2Epng&align=Center&responsive=true}

Metastasis remains the principal cause of mortality among cancer patients. For a tumor cell to metastasize, it must escape the primary tumor, successfully negotiate various molecular and cellular interactions, and colonize a new microenvironment to establish a secondary tumor. To predict how and when cancer will metastasize and to develop more effective treatments, a better understanding is needed about how these individual events - tumor growth, dissemination, colonization, and survival - contribute to the complex metastatic process. Recent advances in live-cell imaging, characterization of circulating tumor cells, experimental models of tumor dormancy, descriptions of tumor cell – immune system crosstalk, cell and tissue mechanics, and single-cell genomic and proteomic analysis have provided quantitative data that can be used to build testable mathematical and computational models of tumor metastasis. 
 
The Interdisciplinary Approaches to Cancer Metastasis workshop, to be held **June 12-14, 2017**, in Seattle, WA at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center, will bring together ~25 early stage investigators (within 15 years of terminal degree) across four NCI-supported programs, the Innovative Molecular Analysis Technologies ([IMAT](https://imat.cancer.gov)) program, the Informatics Technology for Cancer Research ([ITCR](https://itcr.nci.nih.gov)) program, the Cancer Systems Biology Consortium ([CSBC](http://csbconsortium.org)) and the Physical Sciences-Oncology Network ([PS-ON](https://physics.cancer.gov)), along with select outside investigators to tackle important questions in cancer metastasis. The goal is to form teams that utilize the technologies and computational approaches championed by IMAT and ITCR along with the cancer systems biology and physical oncology viewpoints employed within the CSBC and PS-ON. Teams will nucleate around a question in cancer metastasis that can best be addressed through an interdisciplinary approach.
 
Discussions at the workshop will be guided by distinguished scientist “[Mentors](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/wiki/408136),” who will assist in articulating project ideas and facilitate participant discussions both before and during the workshop. Select proposals developed during the Interdisciplinary Approaches to Cancer Metastasis workshop will be selected for funding through a process involving workshop participants, scientific Mentors, and NCI Program Staff. Specific details about the workshop can be found [here](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/wiki/408139).

About the workshop
The IACM workshop is designed to solicit novel pilot project ideas and distribute funds to one or more **teams** of scientists from diverse institutions and backgrounds.  The workshop itself is divided into three stages, as preparation is required of the attendees before the workshop and follow-up is expected from those attendees who receive the pilot project funds.

###Pre-workshop activities
Ahead of the workshop selected applicants will meet weekly ~6 times to discuss ideas with other attendees and describe ideas via teleconference.  All applicants will gain access to [this Synapse project site](syn7433743) to facilitate discussions and brainstorming in between the meetings and ultimately form teams surrounding select ideas. Selected applicants are expected to:
* Register for a [Synapse account](http://www.synapse.org/register) to gain access
* Attend 6 weekly [virtual meetings](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn9693597) with the other selected attendees and selected mentors
* Initiate discussions in the [discussion forum](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/discussion/default) to identify other candidates to form teams
* Work with those teams begin to discuss project ideas and proposals

###Workshop agenda
Selected applicants are invited to Seattle, WA to participate in the workshop June 12-14, 2017.  This will give the attendees the ability to meet their teammates in person and solidify the project proposal with respect to the pilot project funds. Each team will arrive ready to present their ideas to the group and then refine these ideas and establish a budget throughout the workshop. At the end of the workshop each team will present their proposal to use some or all of the pilot project funds (~\$500,000 in total funds). 
 
All workshop attendees will rank the project proposals and the mentors and meeting organizers will use these rankings to select a final division of funds. Depending on the rankings and proposals, all funds may go to a single collaborative team or be divided among multiple teams. 

A more detailed agenda has been posted on the [IACM attendee page](syn9874222).

###Post-workshop followup
The team(s) selected to receive the pilot project funds will be given 1 year to carry out the research as well as modest travel funds to meet amongst themselves and/or present their ideas.

This page describes the pre-workshop activities required by invited attendees to the workshop. The goal of these activities is to facilitate the formation of teams that will be ready to kick-off the workshop with a brief presentation of their proposal, which will then be refined over the two-day workshop.
 
Below are the basic steps to get started: 

###Accessing data portal
This [Synapse Project](http://docs.synapse.org/articles/making_a_project.html) will provide ongoing updates for the workshop as we proceed through the planning activities.  You will require access to the full capabilities of this site to participate in [discussions](http://docs.synapse.org/articles/discussion.html) and make use of the [file sharing capabilities](http://docs.synapse.org/articles/versioning.html).  Specifically you will need to:
* Register for Synapse at http://www.synapse.org/register
* Log into synapse using your registered account (make sure you use your first and last name)
* Join the IACM workshop attendee team by clicking the button below:

You can then begin to create folders under the [IACM Project Workspace](syn8063299) folder. The workshop organizers will host numerous teleconferences that will provide a space for workshop attendees to discuss their ideas with potential team mates as well as workshop organizers.  Links to the teleconferences can be provided [here](syn9693597).

The workshop will kick off with presentations from all teams. More details forthcoming.

The workshop is primarily geared toward early stage investigators, designated as those that are within 15 years of a terminal degree*, who are interested in meeting new collaborators and expanding their current research portfolio. Those investigators that do not yet hold an independent position (i.e. postdoctoral fellow or research scientist) are welcome to apply, although if they are not recognized as Principal Investigators by their Institution they likely will not be eligible to receive pilot project funding.Workshop capacity is set at ~25 attendees, who will be selected from the pool of applicants by the NCI representatives, Sage Bionetworks and the [workshop mentors](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn7433743/wiki/408136).

## HuR-ELAVL1 drives malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor growth and metastasis.

**Disease Focus:** MPNST (Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumor)
**Assay Types:** Bulk RNA-seq, ChIP-seq
**Species:** Homo sapiens
**Tissue / Cell Type:** MPNST cell lines (ST88-14, ST88)
**Publication:** [PMID:32315290](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32315290/) · [DOI:10.1172/JCI130379](https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI130379)
**Authors:** Marta Palomo-Irigoyen, ..., Ashwin Woodhoo
**Institution:** CIC bioGUNE, Basque Research and Technology Alliance (BRTA)
**Publication Date:** 2020 (JCI)

---

### Summary

This study identifies HuR (ELAVL1), an RNA-binding protein, as a key oncogenic driver in MPNSTs. HuR is highly elevated in human MPNST samples and controls a broad transcriptomic program essential for tumor growth and metastasis. Inhibition of HuR exerts potent cytostatic and cytotoxic effects in MPNST cell lines in vitro and suppresses metastasis in vivo.

---

### Background

Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs) are highly aggressive sarcomas arising from Schwann cell lineage cells. They are strongly metastatic, resistant to chemo- and radiotherapy, and frequently fatal. This work demonstrates that MPNST cells develop a strong addiction to the RNA-binding protein HuR/ELAVL1, which coordinates the expression of multiple oncogenic networks, making it an attractive therapeutic target.

# Cellular senescence in human liver under normal aging and cancer

This project accompanies the study by Karpova, Li, Peng, and colleagues in *Cell Genomics* (2026). The paper maps cellular senescence across human liver aging, fibrosis, and colorectal cancer liver metastasis using single-cell and spatial measurements.

**Publication:** Karpova A, Li X, Peng C-W, et al. Cellular senescence in human liver under normal aging and cancer. *Cell Genomics*. 2026;6(2):101133. [DOI: 10.1016/j.xgen.2025.101133](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xgen.2025.101133) · [PubMed: 41576948](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41576948/) · [Open-access article](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12903365/)

## Study overview

The study profiled 43 non-tumor human livers spanning age and fibrosis stages, alongside 24 colorectal cancer liver metastases and complementary mouse models of liver fibrosis. Its assays included single-cell multiome profiling, Xenium spatial transcriptomics, and CODEX imaging.

The authors reported CDKN1A-positive senescence-associated populations among hepatocytes, fibroblasts, cholangiocytes, and endothelial cells. Their spatial analyses identified periportal CDKN1A-positive hepatocytes and CXCL12-positive fibroblasts in fibrotic regions. In the metastatic cancer cohort, recent chemotherapy was associated with substantially more senescence-associated hepatocytes and distinct CDKN2A-positive populations. See the paper for the full results, methods, and limitations.

Improving Immunotherapy in MPNSTs
# Improving Immunotherapy in MPNSTs
## GFF - Next Generation Models
### Principal Investigator: Dawn Quelle
### Project Lead / Data Coordinator: Dawn Quelle, Rebecca Dodd
### Institution: University of Iowa
### Project Description:
Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors (MPNSTs) are the leading cause of death in NF1 patients. Roughly half of MPNST patients develop metastases, and the 5-year survival rate of 20-35% has not improved in the past 30 years. Immunotherapy has revolutionized treatment of common cancers, but MPNSTs are usually resistant to this approach. To determine strategies to improve MPNST response to immunotherapy, rigorously-tested mouse models with active immune systems are needed. We have built a powerful collection of immune-competent MPNST models that reflect patient mutations and model tumor metastasis. Our overall goal is to generate mouse models that can define new therapeutic strategies for NF1 patients. This proposal will test the hypothesis that our mouse models are robust platforms to evaluate immunotherapy strategies for MPNST. These studies are based on exciting preclinical data that have inspired an emerging clinical trial. Using our MPNST models, we identified new targeted therapies that improve tumor response to immunotherapy, with complete cure observed for some tumors. A very similar drug combination is being tested in an upcoming clinical trial. In this proposal, we will examine patient tissue from this clinical trial and our tissue repository to compare immunological and molecular signatures with our mouse model. We will also perform preclinical studies to test improved immunotherapy approaches that can slow or even ablate tumor growth and prevent metastasis in NF1-associated MPNSTs. If successful, these studies will determine how best to use MPNST mouse models to predict clinical response to immunotherapy. Importantly, these types of studies are vital to developing new therapies, but they are rarely funded by federal agencies. Therefore, this Gilbert Foundation Award is a unique opportunity to define the clinical utility of MPNST animal models and determine new immunotherapy strategies for NF1 patients.

**Overview**
[Melanoma Organoid Research](https://www.alfacytology.com/3d-cancer-models/melanoma-organoid-development.html) has become an advanced approach for investigating melanoma biology, tumor progression, metastasis, and therapeutic responses through physiologically relevant three-dimensional (3D) tumor models. Melanoma is one of the most aggressive forms of skin cancer and is characterized by extensive genetic diversity, phenotypic plasticity, metastatic potential, and complex interactions with the tumor microenvironment. Conventional cell culture systems and animal models often cannot fully reproduce the biological complexity of melanoma, while melanoma organoids preserve key characteristics of primary tumors, including genetic alterations, cellular heterogeneity, tissue architecture, and treatment response patterns. (alfacytology.com)

This resource presents an overview of Melanoma Organoid Research using patient-derived melanoma organoids, cell line-derived organoids, genetically engineered organoids, and other advanced 3D melanoma models. By integrating organoid technologies with molecular profiling, functional assays, imaging analysis, and multi-omics approaches, researchers can investigate melanoma mechanisms, evaluate therapeutic strategies, and develop more predictive models for translational oncology and precision medicine research. (alfacytology.com)

**Research Focus**
Melanoma Organoid Research encompasses a broad range of studies focused on melanoma initiation, progression, invasion, metastasis, tumor heterogeneity, and treatment response. Research areas include melanoma molecular characterization, tumor microenvironment analysis, genetic profiling, signaling pathway regulation, biomarker discovery, immune-tumor interactions, and mechanisms associated with therapeutic resistance. (alfacytology.com)

Patient-derived melanoma organoids maintain important genetic and phenotypic features of original tumors, enabling researchers to investigate tumor evolution and patient-specific responses to therapeutic interventions. These models can preserve mutation profiles and cellular diversity associated with melanoma subtypes, providing valuable platforms for studying molecular drivers, tumor adaptation, and genotype-phenotype relationships. (alfacytology.com)

Integrating melanoma organoid models with genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, functional screening, and bioinformatics enables comprehensive investigation of drug sensitivity, resistance mechanisms, and predictive biomarkers. Advanced melanoma organoid systems, including immune cell co-culture models and tumor microenvironment models, further support studies of interactions between melanoma cells, immune components, stromal cells, and extracellular matrix elements. These systems provide valuable platforms for investigating immune evasion mechanisms and evaluating immunotherapeutic strategies within biologically relevant environments. (alfacytology.com)

**Applications**
Melanoma Organoid Research supports a wide range of oncology applications, including melanoma disease modeling, drug screening, therapeutic efficacy evaluation, drug resistance research, biomarker discovery, mechanism-of-action studies, immuno-oncology research, precision medicine, and preclinical drug development. (alfacytology.com)

These organoid-based approaches enable researchers to evaluate targeted therapies, immune-based treatments, combination therapies, and emerging anticancer compounds using biologically relevant melanoma models. By linking molecular characteristics with functional treatment responses, melanoma organoids provide valuable platforms for identifying predictive biomarkers, understanding resistance mechanisms, and optimizing personalized therapeutic strategies. (alfacytology.com)

Melanoma organoid models are also valuable tools for studying tumor invasion and metastasis. Their three-dimensional structure enables researchers to investigate tumor cell migration, adaptation to microenvironmental conditions, and interactions between melanoma cells and surrounding cellular components, providing deeper insights into melanoma progression mechanisms. (alfacytology.com)

As organoid technologies continue to advance, integrating Melanoma Organoid Research with multi-omics characterization, advanced imaging, and functional validation has become increasingly important for modern cancer research. This resource provides researchers with an overview of experimental strategies for establishing representative melanoma models, understanding disease mechanisms, and accelerating the development of innovative therapeutic approaches.

hits.name: Cancer Progression and Metabolic Analysis
hits.description:
# Cancer Progression and Metabolic Analysis

## Overview

[Cancer Progression and Metabolic Analysis](https://www.alfacytology.com/3d-cancer-models/cancer-progression-and-metabolic-analysis.html) is an emerging field of oncology research that investigates the dynamic relationship between tumor progression and metabolic reprogramming. During cancer development, malignant cells continuously adapt their metabolic pathways to sustain rapid proliferation, survive under nutrient- and oxygen-limited conditions, evade immune surveillance, and promote invasion and metastasis. These metabolic adaptations have become recognized as fundamental hallmarks of cancer and represent promising targets for therapeutic intervention.

This resource presents an overview of research strategies for studying cancer progression and metabolic analysis using physiologically relevant three-dimensional tumor models and integrated analytical technologies. By combining advanced organoid systems with molecular, cellular, and functional analyses, researchers can investigate metabolic plasticity, tumor evolution, and the biological mechanisms underlying disease progression in a controlled experimental environment.

## Research Focus

**Cancer Progression and Metabolic Analysis** encompasses the investigation of metabolic pathways and cellular processes that contribute to tumor development and therapeutic response. Research in this area includes the analysis of glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, amino acid metabolism, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, metabolic stress adaptation, and metabolic interactions within the tumor microenvironment. Understanding how these pathways influence tumor growth, invasion, metastasis, and therapy resistance provides valuable insights into cancer biology and translational oncology.

Studies may also examine metabolic crosstalk between tumor cells and stromal cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), immune cells, and endothelial cells to better understand how the tumor microenvironment shapes metabolic behavior. Integrating organoid models with metabolomics, lipidomics, transcriptomics, functional metabolic assays, and multi-omics analyses enables comprehensive characterization of metabolic reprogramming and facilitates the identification of novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

## Applications

**Cancer Progression and Metabolic Analysis** supports a broad spectrum of oncology research applications, including cancer metabolism research, tumor progression studies, metabolic reprogramming analysis, biomarker discovery, drug target validation, mechanism-of-action studies, precision oncology, and preclinical drug development. These research approaches are also valuable for investigating therapeutic resistance, metabolic vulnerabilities, tumor microenvironment interactions, and evaluating innovative anticancer therapies targeting cancer metabolism.

As advances in cancer metabolism continue to reshape oncology research, physiologically relevant three-dimensional tumor models have become increasingly important for reproducing the complexity of tumor biology and metabolic adaptation. Comprehensive cancer progression and metabolic analysis provides researchers with predictive experimental systems for exploring metabolic mechanisms, accelerating translational cancer research, and supporting the development of next-generation therapeutic strategies.

hits.name: Cancer Protein and Signaling Research
hits.description:
**Overview**
[Cancer Protein and Signaling Research](https://www.alfacytology.com/3d-cancer-models/protein-signaling-analysis.html) is a critical field of modern oncology focused on understanding the dynamic protein networks and signaling pathways that regulate tumor initiation, progression, metastasis, and therapeutic response. Unlike genomic alterations, protein expression and post-translational modifications, particularly protein phosphorylation, provide real-time insights into cellular activity and pathway regulation. Investigating these functional molecular events is essential for deciphering cancer biology, identifying therapeutic targets, and advancing precision oncology.

This resource presents an overview of Cancer Protein and Signaling Research using advanced tumor organoids and physiologically relevant three-dimensional (3D) cancer models. By integrating proteomics, phosphoproteomics, multiplex protein profiling, and functional signaling analyses, researchers can characterize pathway activation, evaluate drug responses, and investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying tumor progression and treatment resistance.

**Research Focus**
Cancer Protein and Signaling Research encompasses a broad range of studies investigating protein expression, phosphorylation dynamics, signal transduction, and oncogenic pathway regulation. Research areas include receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling, PI3K/AKT, MAPK/ERK, Wnt/β-catenin, JAK/STAT, NF-κB, TGF-β, and other signaling networks that influence cancer cell proliferation, apoptosis, invasion, metastasis, and immune regulation.

Three-dimensional tumor organoids preserve native tissue architecture, tumor heterogeneity, and cell-cell interactions, providing biologically relevant platforms for functional protein analysis. Integrating organoid models with quantitative proteomics, phosphoproteomics, multiplex immunoassays, mass spectrometry, high-content imaging, and bioinformatics enables researchers to investigate signaling network dynamics, pathway crosstalk, adaptive resistance mechanisms, and molecular responses to targeted therapies within representative tumor microenvironments.

**Applications**
Cancer Protein and Signaling Research supports a wide range of oncology applications, including cancer proteomics, phosphoproteomics, signal transduction research, biomarker discovery, pathway activity profiling, drug target validation, mechanism-of-action studies, precision oncology, and preclinical drug development. These research approaches also facilitate investigations into therapeutic resistance, predictive biomarker identification, pathway inhibition, and combination therapy evaluation using advanced 3D cancer models.

As proteomics technologies and signaling analyses continue to evolve, integrating Cancer Protein and Signaling Research with physiologically relevant tumor organoid models has become increasingly important for translational cancer research. This resource provides researchers with an overview of experimental strategies for characterizing protein signaling networks, understanding functional pathway regulation, and accelerating the development of innovative targeted therapies and personalized cancer treatments.

**Angiogenesis and Lymphangiogenesis Analysis**

**Overview**

[Angiogenesis and Lymphangiogenesis Analysis](https://www.alfacytology.com/3d-cancer-models/angiogenesis-and-lymphangiogenesis-analysis.html) is a critical area of cancer research focused on understanding how blood vessel and lymphatic vessel formation contribute to tumor growth, progression, metastasis, and therapeutic response. Angiogenesis supplies tumors with oxygen and nutrients required for continuous growth, while lymphangiogenesis facilitates the dissemination of cancer cells through the lymphatic system. Together, these dynamic vascular processes play fundamental roles in shaping the tumor microenvironment and have become important targets in oncology research and drug development.

This resource provides an overview of research approaches for investigating angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis using advanced three-dimensional tumor models and integrated analytical strategies. By combining physiologically relevant experimental systems with molecular, morphological, and functional analyses, researchers can better characterize vascular remodeling and tumor-endothelial interactions throughout cancer progression.

**Research Focus**

Angiogenesis and Lymphangiogenesis Analysis encompasses the quantitative and functional evaluation of vascular development within the tumor microenvironment. Research in this field investigates endothelial cell behavior, vascular network formation, vessel branching, lumen development, vascular permeability, extracellular matrix remodeling, hypoxia, and the signaling pathways that regulate angiogenic and lymphangiogenic processes.

Studies may also explore the interactions between tumor cells, endothelial cells, lymphatic endothelial cells, immune cells, and stromal components that collectively influence tumor invasion and metastatic dissemination. Molecular characterization of angiogenic regulators, including VEGF signaling pathways and other vascular biomarkers, together with high-resolution imaging and three-dimensional morphometric analysis, provides valuable insights into the mechanisms driving vascular remodeling and cancer progression.

**Applications**

Angiogenesis and Lymphangiogenesis Analysis supports a wide range of oncology research applications, including tumor microenvironment characterization, vascular biology research, cancer progression studies, metastasis research, immuno-oncology, biomarker discovery, drug target validation, mechanism-of-action studies, and preclinical drug development. These research approaches also enable the evaluation of anti-angiogenic therapies, vascular-targeted drug candidates, combination treatment strategies, and therapeutic responses using physiologically relevant tumor models.

As the understanding of tumor vascular biology continues to advance, comprehensive angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis analysis has become increasingly important for translational cancer research. Integrating three-dimensional tumor models with quantitative vascular analysis provides researchers with more predictive experimental systems for investigating tumor-endothelial interactions and accelerating the development of innovative anticancer therapies.

Challenge Overview
In the HeLP Challenge, we will host data consisting of medical data (i.e., X-ray, CT, digital pathology images, and numeric data) and corresponding clinical information. The goal of the HeLP Challenge is to apply an open science, crowdsourced approach to developing algorithms for several classification and detection tasks. 
 
The HeLP Challenge will utilize deidentified medical images and clinical datasets made available for research by Asan Medical Center (AMC) and Seoul National University Bundang Hospital (SNUBH). Challenge participants will use this data to develop classification or detection models that address the specific questions posed by Challenge organizers (sub-contest). The submitted models will be objectively scored using a test set (that Challenge participants are unable to access), with scores posted on the Challenge leaderboard. For each sub-contest, the Challenge participant or team with the best performing algorithm will be declared the (1st and 2nd) winners and the cash prize will be awarded. After winners of all sub-contests were declared, they will be invited to participate in the Challenge wrap up workshop. At the workshop, each team will be invited to present their method and results and the best presenters will award GPUs for the deep learning development. All winners (or more participants) will be invited to co-author a publication describing the results of the Challenge analyses and highlighting their team methodologies and results.

1.1. Scientific overview
흉부 X-ray는 환자의 심장혈관이상 및 동반된 폐질환을 발견하기 위해 1차적으로 시행하는 매우 기본적인 검사이다. 흉부 X-ray는 CT나 MRI에 비하면 관찰할 수 있는 구조물에 제한이 있고, 심장 및 혈관의 변화가 심하지 않으면 이상소견을 발견하지 못할 수도 있다는 단점이 있지만, CT나 MRI보다 값이 저렴하고 검사방법도 간단하기 때문에 쉽게 검사할 수 있는 장점이 있다. 흉부 X-ray에서 심장 및 대혈관의 이상의 진단은 심혈관경계선 (Cardiovascular border; 이하 CB)의 변화를 전문가가 보고 판단하는 방법에 의존한다. 

${image?fileName=CB%5Ffig1%2Ejpg&align=None&scale=50&responsive=false&altText=}

심혈관경계선 (CB)는 심장의 각 분분 및 대혈관과 대응되기 때문에 CB의 변화를 감지하면 심장 및 대혈관의 어떤 부분이 변화하였는지 추측이 가능하다. 하지만 이러한 변화들은 다른 질환 (예, 종격동의 종괴)과 중복되는 소견일수 있고, 실제 이상이 있더라도 CB의 변화로 나타나지 않는 경우도 많아서 영상 판독의 전문가인 영상의학과 전문의들조차도 CB의 변화에 따른 심혈관질환의 진단에 익숙하지 않은 경우가 많다. 심혈관의 진단의 이상을 진단하는 지표가운데 대표적이면서 비교적 간단한 방법은 Cardiothoracic Ratio (CT ratio)라는 것인데 이는 다음과 같은 공식으로 간단히 구할 수 있고 0.5가 정상 상한치로 알려져 있다: (maximal transverse cardiac silhouette diameter) / (maximal internal thoracic diameter). 하지만 CT ratio는 다양한 심혈관질환의 이상을 반영하기에는 너무 간단한 지표라는 제한점이 있다. 따라서 판독을 담당하는 영상의학과 전문의들도 대부분은 폐나 흉막의 이상이나 뼈의 이상소견에 집중하는 경향이 많다. 이에 따라 흉부 X-ray의 자동진단을 목표로 하는인공지능의 개발도 폐질환 (nodule, consolidation), 흉막질환 (pneumothorax, pleural effusion), 뼈의 이상 (rib fracture, vertebral fracture)등에 집중되는 경우가 많다.

만약 인공지능 알고리즘이 CB를 자동으로 검출할 수 있다면 어떨까? 기존에는 의사들의 ‘심장 음영이 큰 것 같다’ 다소 주관적인 판단에 의해 진단하였다면 각 CB의 변화를 정량화 함으로써 정상 및 다양한 질환의 보다 객관적인 진단에 도움을 줄 수 있을 것이다. 또한 CB의 시간에 따른 변화를 객관적으로 볼 수 있다면 흉부 X-ray에서 심혈관 진단을 조금 더 잘 진단하는데 유용한 도구가 될 수 있을 것이다.

2.1. Scientific overview
Trauma is the main cause of death and has a significant impact on the patient's life and health system. 'Golden hour' is a term commonly used in trauma, which indicates that an injured patient has 60 minutes from time of injury to receive definitive care, after which morbidity and mortality significantly increase. The shorter the time to definite care after a serious injury, the higher the chance of survival. Computed tomography (CT) is essential for the evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment planning of these patients; however, trauma patients often present with multiple injuries, requiring a whole body scan, which can take time to acquire and analyze whole body images. Recent technological advances in CT equipment have saved a great deal of time for fast image acquisition and reconstruction, but the interpretation of images is still a problem. In terms of the golden hour, automatic classification and detection of traumatic lesions using deep learning model can provide emergency/trauma physicians and surgeons with diagnoses in the shortest possible time.

2.4. Evaluation matrix
In order that	this challenge appraises algorithms for both trauma patients’ classification and traumatic lesion localization/detection, the following three strategies will be used to evaluate the performance of the algorithms.

**Per-patient evaluation**
For discriminating between patients containing traumatic lesions and normal patients, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis at the patient level will be performed and the measure used for comparing the algorithms will be the area under the ROC (AUC).

**Per-slice evaluation**
In the same manner as the per-patient evaluation, ROC analysis at the slice level will be performed and the measure used for comparing the algorithms will be the AUC.

**Per-lesion evaluation**
For the lesion-based evaluation, free-response receiver operating characteristic (FROC) curve will be used. The FROC curve is defined as the plot of sensitivity versus the average number of false-positives per image.

**Total score**
Each task is evaluated by adding up the results of each traumatic lesion with different weights – Hemothorax: 20%, Pneumothorax: 30%, and Hemoperitoneum: 50%. Finally, rank is determined by weighted sum of the result of three tasks – task 1. per-patient evaluation: 20%, task 2. per-slice evaluation: 30%, and task 3. Per-lesion evaluation: 50%.

3.1. Scientific overview
Assessing the status of metastasis in sentinel lymph nodes (SLNs) by pathologists is an essential task for the accurate staging of breast cancer. However, histopathological evaluation of sentinel lymph nodes by a pathologist is a tedious and time-consuming task. Furthermore, pathologists sometimes must evaluate SLNs by intraoperative consultation using FROZEN tissue sections.
The Cancer Metastases in Lymph Nodes Challenge 2016 (CAMELYON16) competition disclosed that some deep learning algorithms achieved better diagnostic performance than a panel of 11 pathologists participating in a simulation exercise designed to mimic routine pathology workflow. We held HeLP Challenge 2018 to know the performance of automated deep learning algorithms at detecting metastases in hematoxylin and eosin–stained FROZEN tissue sections of SLNs in breast cancer patients. In HeLP Challenge 2019, we have expanded our dataset and aim not only to determine presence of metastasis but also to measure the longest diameter of metastatic tumors.

4.1. Scientific overview
최근 산모의 고령화와 불임 치료 기술의 발달, 환경 유해 인자 증가 등으로 인해 미숙아 출생이 증가하고 치료 기술의 발달로 미숙아를 비롯한 고위험 신생아들의 생존률이 크게 증가하고 있다. 그러나 미성숙한 환자의 방어면역기전과 다양한 침습적 처치의 증가로 인해 감염 발생 위험이 크게 증가하고 신생아중환자실(neonatal intensive care unit, NICU)에서 의료관련감염은 출생 초기의 위중한 상태를 극복한 미숙아들이 직면하는 가장 심각한 위협이 되고 있다. 
미숙아에게 주로 발생하는 감염 질환 및 유병요인으로는 괴사성 장염(necrotizing enterocolitis, NEC), 패혈증(sepsis), 저혈압(hypotension) 등이 있으며 이를 조기에 예측하여 발견하고 초기에 적절한 치료가 이루어지면 미숙아의 사망률을 크게 낮출 ���가 있다. 이미 인공지능을 이용하여 질병을 예방하고 예측하는 연구들이 다양하게 진행되고 있다. 한 예로 존스 홉킨스 의과대학의 연구진은 중환자실 환자를 대상으로 전자의무기록에 매일 기록되는 체온, 호흡수, 심장박동수, 혈압 등의 일상 데이터를 바탕으로 패혈성 쇼크의 위험이 높은 환자를 예측할 수 있는 실시간 조기 경고 점수를 개발했다. 

${image?fileName=NICU%5Ffig1%2Ejpg&align=None&scale=90&responsive=false&altText=}
사실 중환자실에는 환자들의 상태를 모니터링하기 위해 다양한 생체신호 데이터를 측정한다. 하지만 1초에서 수천개의 데이터가 쌓일 정도로 방대한 데이터이기 때문에 기존 병원 시스템에서는 이 데이터가 저장되지 못하고 버려지기 마련이다. 하지만 환자의 질병 및 증상을 예측하는 알고리즘이 실제 임상에서 활용되기 위해서는 많은 수의 환자에 대해서 다양한 생체신호 데이터를 지속적으로 측정하고 저장되며 ���시간으로 분석할 수 있어야 한다. 이런 일환으로 본 챌린지에서는 신생아중환자실의 입원 환자들을 통해 실시간으로 측정되어 30초 단위로 수집된 생체신호(혈압, 맥박, 산호포화도 등)와 임상 데이터를 활용하여 예측 알고리즘을 개발하고자 한다. 

4.2. Challenge questions
참가자는 NICU에 입원해 있는 미숙아의 생체 신호와 기본 환자 정보를 기반으로 critical event가 발생하기 전에 진단, 예측하여 의료진이 사전 중재 및 예방할 수 있도록 해야 한다.
Critical event는 패혈증(Neonatal sepsis), 저혈압(Hypotension), 괴사성 장염(Necrotizing enterocolitis), 사망으로 정의한다.
예측 모델은 2가지의 작업을 수행해야 한다.
- 미숙아 입원 후 1 시간 단위 주기로 측정된 시점에서 해당 미숙아가 12시간 이내로 중증 상태 조건에 진입했는지 여부 (t~event~-12hr ≤ t~current~ ≤ t~event~ 일 경우 positive)
- 미숙아 입원 후 1 시간 단위 주기로 측정된 시점에서 해당 미숙아가 6시간 이내로 중증 상태 조건에 진입했는지 여부 (t~event~-6hr ≤ t~current~ ≤ t~event~ 일 경우 positive)

4.3. Data description
본 데이터는 단일기관(분당서울대학교병원)에서 중증 미숙아 예측 모델의 training, testing, validation 을 수행하기 위해 9개월 동안 수집된 데이터이다. 

**Study Population**
전체 연구 대상 환자군은 9개월 기간의 NICU 입원 환자 중 재태연령 32주 미만 또는 출생 체중 1500g 인 미숙아 107명을 대상으로 데이터가 수집되었다. 이 중 47명이 critical event가 발생하였다.

**Acquisition protocol**
미숙아의 생체신호는 Philips 사의 patient monitor에서 HL7 message 형식의 데이터를 가공하여 수집하였으며, 평균 30초 주기로 한번씩 기록된다. 수집 데이터 중 환자의 이름과 생일 등의 개인 정보들은 수집 대상에서 제외되며 아래 테이블의 혈압, 심박수와 같은 생체 신호만을 대상으로 하였다.

hits.description:
**Overview**
[Cholangiocarcinoma Organoid Research](https://www.alfacytology.com/3d-cancer-models/cholangiocarcinoma-organoid-development.html) has become an advanced approach for investigating cholangiocarcinoma biology, tumor progression, and therapeutic responses through physiologically relevant three-dimensional (3D) tumor models. Cholangiocarcinoma is an aggressive malignancy originating from the biliary tract and is characterized by extensive molecular heterogeneity, complex tumor microenvironment interactions, and limited therapeutic options. Conventional experimental models often fail to fully reproduce the biological complexity of cholangiocarcinoma, while cholangiocarcinoma organoids preserve important characteristics of primary tumors, including cellular heterogeneity, glandular architecture, genetic alterations, and molecular profiles, providing valuable platforms for translational cancer research. 

This resource presents an overview of Cholangiocarcinoma Organoid Research using patient-derived organoids (PDOs), tumor tissue-derived organoids, genetically engineered organoids, and other advanced 3D cholangiocarcinoma models. By integrating organoid technologies with molecular profiling, functional assays, imaging analysis, and multi-omics approaches, researchers can investigate cholangiocarcinoma mechanisms, evaluate therapeutic responses, and develop more predictive models for precision oncology and preclinical drug development. 

**Research Focus**
Cholangiocarcinoma Organoid Research encompasses a broad range of studies focused on bile duct cancer initiation, progression, invasion, metastasis, tumor heterogeneity, and therapeutic response. Research areas include intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC) modeling, extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma characterization, genetic profiling, signaling pathway regulation, tumor microenvironment analysis, metabolic alterations, biomarker discovery, and mechanisms associated with drug resistance. 

Patient-derived cholangiocarcinoma organoids retain key molecular and phenotypic features of original tumors, enabling researchers to investigate disease evolution and patient-specific therapeutic responses. These models can preserve tumor architecture, cellular diversity, and molecular characteristics, making them valuable platforms for studying cholangiocarcinoma pathogenesis and identifying potential therapeutic targets. 

Integrating cholangiocarcinoma organoid models with genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and bioinformatics enables comprehensive investigation of driver mutations, signaling pathways, metabolic reprogramming, drug sensitivity, and resistance mechanisms. These approaches provide insights into how molecular alterations contribute to tumor growth, disease progression, and treatment response. 

Advanced cholangiocarcinoma organoid systems, including co-culture models incorporating stromal cells, immune cells, endothelial cells, and extracellular matrix components, further support research into tumor-stroma interactions and the tumor microenvironment. These models provide physiologically relevant platforms for studying immune regulation, invasion, metastasis, and therapeutic responses. 

**Applications**
Cholangiocarcinoma Organoid Research supports a broad range of oncology applications, including cholangiocarcinoma disease modeling, drug screening, therapeutic efficacy evaluation, drug resistance research, biomarker discovery, mechanism-of-action studies, precision medicine, and preclinical drug development. 

These organoid-based approaches enable researchers to evaluate anticancer compounds, targeted therapies, and combination treatment strategies using biologically relevant cholangiocarcinoma models. By linking molecular characteristics with functional drug responses, cholangiocarcinoma organoids provide valuable platforms for identifying predictive biomarkers and optimizing personalized therapeutic approaches. 

Cholangiocarcinoma organoid models are particularly valuable for studying tumor metabolism and therapeutic resistance. These models allow researchers to investigate metabolic changes that support tumor survival, identify mechanisms underlying treatment failure, and evaluate potential strategies for overcoming resistance.

As organoid technologies continue to advance, integrating Cholangiocarcinoma Organoid Research with multi-omics characterization, advanced imaging, and functional validation has become increasingly important for modern hepatobiliary oncology research. This resource provides researchers with an overview of experimental strategies for establishing representative cholangiocarcinoma models, understanding disease mechanisms, and accelerating the development of innovative therapeutic approaches.

**Overview**
[Pancreatic Cancer Organoid Research](https://www.alfacytology.com/3d-cancer-models/pancreatic-cancer-organoid-development.html) has become an advanced approach for investigating pancreatic cancer biology, tumor progression, and therapeutic responses through physiologically relevant three-dimensional (3D) tumor models. Pancreatic cancer, particularly pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), is characterized by aggressive progression, extensive molecular heterogeneity, and a highly complex tumor microenvironment, creating significant challenges for conventional cancer research models. Pancreatic cancer organoids preserve important genetic, phenotypic, and histological characteristics of primary tumors, providing representative platforms for studying disease mechanisms and supporting translational oncology research.

This resource presents an overview of Pancreatic Cancer Organoid Research using patient-derived organoids (PDOs), genetically engineered organoids, and other advanced 3D pancreatic cancer models. By integrating organoid technologies with molecular characterization, functional assays, imaging analysis, and multi-omics approaches, researchers can investigate pancreatic tumor development, evaluate therapeutic responses, and establish predictive models for precision oncology and drug discovery.

**Research Focus**
Pancreatic Cancer Organoid Research encompasses a broad range of studies focused on pancreatic tumor initiation, progression, metastasis, and treatment response. Research areas include pancreatic cancer organoid development, tumor heterogeneity analysis, genetic profiling, signaling pathway investigation, cancer stem cell biology, metabolic regulation, biomarker discovery, and tumor microenvironment research.

Patient-derived pancreatic cancer organoids maintain key molecular characteristics and patient-specific features of original tumors, making them valuable platforms for investigating genotype-phenotype relationships and personalized therapeutic strategies. Integrating pancreatic cancer organoids with genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, functional screening, and bioinformatics enables researchers to study tumor evolution, drug sensitivity, resistance mechanisms, and molecular drivers of pancreatic cancer progression.

Advanced pancreatic cancer organoid systems, including organoid co-culture models, organoid-on-a-chip platforms, and tumor microenvironment models, enable researchers to investigate interactions between tumor cells and key stromal components such as cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), immune cells, endothelial cells, and extracellular matrix components. These models provide valuable tools for studying stromal regulation, immune evasion, invasion, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance mechanisms in biologically relevant environments.

**Applications**
Pancreatic Cancer Organoid Research supports a wide range of oncology applications, including pancreatic cancer disease modeling, drug screening, therapeutic efficacy evaluation, drug resistance research, biomarker discovery, mechanism-of-action studies, precision oncology, and preclinical drug development. These organoid-based approaches enable researchers to evaluate candidate therapeutics, investigate treatment responses, and identify potential therapeutic targets using representative pancreatic tumor models.

Pancreatic cancer organoids also provide valuable platforms for personalized medicine research by linking patient-specific molecular characteristics with functional drug responses. Through integration with multi-omics profiling and high-throughput screening approaches, researchers can investigate predictive biomarkers, optimize treatment strategies, and improve the translational relevance of preclinical cancer studies.

As organoid technologies continue to advance, integrating Pancreatic Cancer Organoid Research with advanced molecular analysis and functional validation has become increasingly important for modern oncology research. This resource provides researchers with an overview of experimental strategies for establishing representative pancreatic cancer models, understanding disease mechanisms, and accelerating the development of innovative therapeutic approaches.

hits.description:
#CBTC Challenge 3: Guess the Primary
This is the third of three Challenges in the Computational Brain Tumor Cluster of Events ([CBTC](https://wiki.cancerimagingarchive.net/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=20644646)) 2015 to be held on Oct 9 in Munich, Germany, in conjunction with [MICCAI 2015](http://www.miccai2015.org).

###Challenge Objective
The motivating goal of this Challenge is to study imaging phenotypes of metastatic disease originating from different primary cancers in the body.  We challenge the image segmentation community to determine if primary cancers create distinct imaging signatures that can be automatically detected with segmentation and feature set extraction algorithms. The impact of successfully classifying the histology of the primary tumor based on features of the brain metastasis would be to provide a biological insight into brain tumor imaging and segmentation that could result in improved clinical treatment decisions.

**The objective of this Challenge is to correctly classify metastatic lesions in the brain into lesions resulting from primary cancer from the lung or from the skin (melanoma) using MRI T1+Gadolinium contrast images. **There are 57 image sets in the training data, some with additional sequences beyond T1+Gd. The result set will be a 57x1 vector of predictions that indicate lung or melanoma primary lesion type.

Through this exercise, challenge participants will apply and/or develop algorithms to analyze imaging features and connect them to disease histology.  Based on feature sets identified in these algorithms we hope to gain insight into the underlying biology and growth patterns of metastatic lesions, and perhaps their proclivity to seed and grow differently based on the inherent phenotype they carry with them from the primary cancer organ/site.  

To participate in the Challenge, please visit the [How to Participate page](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn4112414/wiki/234738).

_Questions about the workshop and Challenges? Send email to: Russell Rockne, rrockne@coh.org_

Further instructions will be sent by email.&successMessage=Your registration is in progress.  Further instructions will be sent by email.}

###Step 2. Access the data
Brief descriptions of how to download the data are provided here:
**Web-based download**: You can individually download data files from the project Web page/File tab [here](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn4112414/files/). Select a data file (or folder) and open the associated file Web page by clicking the file name in the file directory. Click on the download icon represented by the downward pointing arrow beside the data file name. This will download the file onto your local computer, likely in your ‘Downloads’ folder.

**Data Access through the R or Python Clients**: You can also access these data through the Synapse Client in R or Python using the scripts provided. The [Synapse User Guide](https://www.synapse.org/#!Wiki:syn1669771/ENTITY) provides instructions and information on accessing Synapse through the R and Python clients.

####Data 
A total of 87 brain MRI image sets are available for this challenge. The [training data](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn4808480) consist of a subset of 57 image sets along with binary masks that segment the image into tumor-positive (1) and tumor-negative (0) pixels that were obtained by trained raters and spot-checked for accuracy by a United States board-certified radiologist. Division of scans into training and test sets was performed pseudo randomly such that data from both lung and melanoma primary disease settings were included in both the training and testing sets. The data are in the NIfTI file format with gzip compression and are arranged as follows:

* ImageSetX (where  1 ≤ X ≤ 87)
   * MRI Modality (ex. T1Gd, FLAIR, T2)
      * mask%.nii.gz
      * MRI%.nii.gz

Each ImageSet is an MRI study with one or more modalities (T1Gd, T2, FLAIR). ImageSets may be repeat scans from the same patient on a different date (i.e., there are not 87 unique patients). The Mask and MRI image sets are of the same dimensions. _It is possible that some of the segmented masks may need to be left-right flipped in the horizontal (axial) plane to align with the MRI when analyzed in MATLAB._ The answer key for the training data is provided in the file [TRAINING-SET-KEY.csv](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn4844059).

The entire training data set is also available for download as a single file, ["TRAINING_SET.tar.gz"](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn4809781)

The remaining 30 image sets will be used for testing and validation.

**Formatting the submission**
Please first format your submission for valid scoring. Please create a comma-separated (CSV) file with the ImageSet id in the first column and your prediction in the second column ("Lung" or "Melanoma") by following the convention in the training set key.  

Submission instructions will be released September 15th with the test data set.

###Step 4. Submit challenge-related abstract

We will host a discussion session on methods and applications used by Challenge participants on Friday October 9th at the [CBTC](https://wiki.cancerimagingarchive.net/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=20644646) satellite event. Please submit your methods abstract to Russell Rockne [rrockne@coh.org](mailto:rrockne@coh.org) by October 1st, 2015. 

**If challenge participants use proprietary algorithms, software, or approaches, details can be omitted. The approach should be described in general terms. **

A template for Challenge abstracts can be found [here](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn4112414/wiki/234783).

Overview



###Background
Over 200,000 people in the US are diagnosed with brain tumors each year, of which 75% are secondary from systemic cancers such as melanoma and lung cancer and are called brain metastases (mets)${reference?inlineWidget=true&text=Surveillance%2C Epidemiology%2C and End Results %28SEER%29 Program Research Data %281973%2D2011%29%2C National Cancer Institute%2C DCCPS%2C Surveillance Research Program%2C Surveillance Systems Branch%2C released April 2014%2C based on the November 2013 submission at www%2Eseer%2Ecancer%2Egov}. Brain mets are a complication that occurs in about 40% of patients with systemic cancer and, when present, are typically the causes of mortality ${reference?inlineWidget=true&text=Linskey%2C Mark E%2E%2C et al%2E "The role of stereotactic radiosurgery in the management of patients with newly diagnosed brain metastases%3A a systematic review and evidence%2Dbased clinical practice guideline%2E" Journal of neuro%2Doncology 96%2E1 %282010%29%3A 45%2D68%2E}.  Historically, brain mets have been treated the same regardless of the primary cancer; however, optimal treatment may vary with histology. We hypothesize that biological differences between primary cancers might lead to distinct radiographic features on MRI for the secondary, or metastatic cancer. One such example could be co-optive or classical mechanisms of angiogenesis ${reference?inlineWidget=true&text=Kienast%2C Yvonne%2C et al%2E "Real%2Dtime imaging reveals the single steps of brain metastasis formation%2E" Nature medicine 16%2E1 %282010%29%3A 116%2D122%2E}, which may be detectable in contrast-enhanced MRI. We challenge the image segmentation community to determine if primary cancers create distinct radiographic signatures that can be automatically detected with segmentation algorithms. # **iS2C2: A Co-Intelligent Platform for Mechanistic Discovery of Disease Cellular Crosstalk**

## **Overview**

This project contains the single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets used to validate the **iS2C2** platform. The study focuses on characterizing the cellular composition, transcriptional programs, and spatial organization of the bone metastatic microenvironment.

**Dataset Title:** Single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomic Profiling of the Bone Metastatic Microenvironment

### **Abstract**

The goal of this study is to comprehensively characterize the cellular composition, transcriptional programs, and spatial organization of the bone metastatic microenvironment and to assess how therapeutic perturbation influences tumor–microenvironment interactions.

A mouse bone metastasis model was established via internal iliac artery injection of Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC1) cells, and metastatic lesions were monitored by *in vivo* imaging. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and 10x Genomics Visium–based spatial transcriptomics were generated from metastatic bone tissues to provide complementary cellular and spatial resolution.

## **Methods**

### **1. Study Design & Animal Models**

* **Growth Protocol:** Mouse bone metastasis samples were generated using an internal iliac artery (IIA) injection model. Mice were maintained under standard laboratory housing conditions with *ad libitum* access to food and water. Bone metastases were induced by injection of LLC1 tumor cells. Animals were monitored post-procedure until full recovery and bone tissues were harvested at defined experimental endpoints.
* **Treatment Protocol:** Bone metastasis was established by IIA injection of LLC1 cells suspended in PBS. Under anesthesia, a surgical incision exposed the common iliac artery, and tumor cells were injected using a 31-gauge needle. Hemostasis and surgical closure followed. Tumor progression was monitored using IVIS imaging. No additional pharmacological treatments were applied unless otherwise specified.

### **2. Sample Extraction**

* **For scRNA-seq:** Bone metastatic tissues were carefully dissected, mechanically minced, and enzymatically dissociated under controlled conditions to preserve cell viability. The resulting suspensions were filtered to remove debris and aggregates, washed, and counted prior to library preparation (refer to *Xu et al., bioRxiv, 2024* for full details).
* **For Spatial Transcriptomics:** Bone tissues were freshly harvested and processed according to the 10x Genomics Visium Spatial Gene Expression protocol (CG000240, Rev A). When necessary, tissues were decalcified using an RNA-preserving EDTA-based protocol prior to embedding in OCT, snap-freezing, and cryosectioning onto Visium slides.

### **3. Library Construction**

* **scRNA-seq:** Libraries were prepared using the **10x Genomics Chromium Single Cell 3′ Gene Expression** platform. Single cells were encapsulated into GEMs, followed by reverse transcription, cDNA amplification, and library construction.
* **Spatial Transcriptomics:** Libraries were generated using the **10x Genomics Visium Spatial Gene Expression** protocol. Tissue sections were fixed, stained, imaged, permeabilized, and reverse-transcribed on-slide. Spatially barcoded cDNA was collected and converted into sequencing libraries.

### **4. Data Processing**

All data was aligned to the mouse reference genome **GRCm38 (mm10)**.

#### **Single-cell RNA-seq Analysis**

* **Preprocessing:** Raw FASTQ files were processed using **Cell Ranger v7.1.0**.
* **QC & Filtering:** Cells with <200 or >2,500 detected genes, or >5% mitochondrial gene content, were excluded.
* **Normalization:** Seurat’s `LogNormalize` (scale factor 10,000) followed by log transformation.
* **Clustering:** Dimensionality reduction via PCA, followed by graph-based clustering (`FindClusters`) and UMAP visualization. Cell types were annotated based on established marker genes.

#### **Spatial Transcriptomics Analysis**

* **Preprocessing:** FASTQ files processed using **Space Ranger v2.1.0**.
* **Integration:** Four samples were integrated using Seurat’s `FindIntegrationAnchors` with reciprocal PCA (RPCA) and mutual nearest neighbors (MNN) to correct for batch effects.
* **Visualization:** Dimensionality reduction (PCA) and UMAP were performed consistent with the scRNA-seq workflow.

---

## **Data Availability**

This project provides the fully processed and annotated datasets used in the study. The data is provided as R objects (`.rds` format) compatible with **Seurat**, containing raw counts, normalized data, dimensionality reduction coordinates (PCA, UMAP), and final cluster/cell-type annotations.

### **Files**

* **`Bone_Mets_scRNAseq.rds`**
* **Description:** The integrated and annotated Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) dataset.
* **Contents:** Includes the gene-barcode matrix, cell-level metadata (niche labels, cell types), and UMAP coordinates.
* **Format:** Seurat Object (R)


* **`Bone_Mets_Spatial_Transcriptomics.rds`**
* **Description:** The integrated Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) dataset.
* **Contents:** Includes spot-by-gene expression matrices, spatial coordinates, image data, and cluster assignments.
* **Format:** Seurat Object (R)



### **How to Load Data in R**

To access the data, download the files and use the following commands in R:

```r
library(Seurat)

# Load Single-Cell Data
sc_data <- readRDS("path/to/sc_object.rds")

# Load Spatial Data
st_data <- readRDS("path/to/s2c2_st_public.rds")

```
